The quantity  $\Xi(N)$  will appear numerous times throughout the paper, so we would like to relate it to the critical window  $\textrm{W}(N)$ . We show a slightly stronger result which will be useful to us later. Recall that  $\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)$  is the modified critical window, given by
$\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)=\textrm{W}(N)\left(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\right)^{-1/2}.$
The following lemma is a simple computation, whose proof is postponed to the Appendix.
Lemma 2.12.
There is some constant  $c>0$  such that one has the following inequalities
$\textrm{W}(N)N^{c}\lesssim\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{2/3}\lesssim\Xi(N).$
2.4 Derivatives of events for non-translation invariant environments
The overall approach that we take in the present paper is to deform continuously, via a continuous family of bonds  $\mathfrak{p}(s)$ , all the edge weights from the critical homogeneous setup at  $p_{c}$  towards the set of weights  $\mathfrak{p}$ . In the deterministic setup, at criticality and below the characteristic length, the strong box-crossing property allows us to deduce all relations recalled inside Theorems 2.2 and 2.3. As time evolves along the deformation process, the fact that some  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  property remains true (with high probability) for the set of weights  $\mathfrak{p}(s)$  ensures that
Proposition 2.4 remains true for the weights  $\mathfrak{p}(s)$  and with all involved quantities remaining the same as the homogeneous ones up to multiplicative constant. Therefore, one can run some infinitesimal deformation from the weights  $\mathfrak{p}(s)$  to  $\mathfrak{p}(s+ds)$ , which implies in return that  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  holds at time  $s+ds$ , implying in return Proposition 2.4 for the weights  $\mathfrak{p}(s+ds)$ .
One can now compute explicitly the derivatives of different quantities with respect to each edge bond  $p_{e}$ . The proof of the following proposition is given in Appendix A.1.
Proposition 2.13.
Given an edge  $e$  in  $E_{N}$ , under the measure  $\phi_{\underline{p}}=\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p},q}$ , the derivatives of the probability of an event  $A$  occurring in  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$  are given by
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[A]$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})}\textrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(A,\omega_{e}),$
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{e}^{2}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[A]$
$\displaystyle=\frac{2}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p_{e}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\right)\textrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(A,\omega_{e}).$
Furthermore, if  $e,f,g$  are three edges in  $E_{N}$ , the derivatives of  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$  are given by
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{g}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{g}(1-p_{g})}\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g),$
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{g}^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$
$\displaystyle=\frac{2}{p_{g}(1-p_{g})^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p_{g}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\right)\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g)$
$\displaystyle\quad-\frac{2}{p_{g}^{2}(1-p_{g})^{2}}\textrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\textrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g}),$
where  $\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g)$  is the third cumulant of the variables  $\omega_{e},\omega_{f},\omega_{g}$  and is given by
$\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g):=\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}\omega_{f}\omega_{g}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}\omega_{f}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}\omega_{g}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}\omega_{g}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\\
+2\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]$
(2.27)
2.5 Geometric estimates in near-critical environments
In this section, we gather estimates on the averaged sums over  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$  of  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})$ ,  $\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g)$  and  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})$  for some environment  $\underline{p}$  which is near-critical (in a sense made precise below). The first natural near-criticality condition on the environment is that  $\underline{p}$  is that the measure  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p}}$  satisfies  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  for some  $\delta>0$ . Still, we require slightly more here, namely that arm events and mixing rates do not degenerate too much from the critical measure. Hence, we define the following for  $\delta>0$  and  $\#\in\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\textrm{rg}},3^{\textrm{lf}}\}$ ,
$\displaystyle\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(\delta,N)$
$\displaystyle:=\left\{\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p},q}\ \Bigg|\ \forall e\in E,\ \forall~1\leq r\leq R\leq N/4,\quad\frac{\pi^{(e)}_{\#,\underline{p}}(r,R)}{\pi_{\#,p_{c}}(r,R)}\in[\delta,1/\delta]\right\},$
$\displaystyle\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\delta,N)$
$\displaystyle:=\left\{\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p},q}\ \Bigg|\ \forall e\in E,\ \forall~1\leq r\leq R\leq N/4,\quad\frac{\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(e)}(r,R)}{\Delta_{p_{c}}(r,R)}\in[\delta,1/\delta]\right\}.$
In the rest of this section, one assumes that
$\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p},q}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\cap\left(\bigcap_{\#\in\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\textrm{rg}},3^{\textrm{lf}}\}}\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(\delta,N)\right)\cap\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\delta,N).$
(2.28)
If the measure  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p},q}$  indeed satisfies (2.28), then it is straightforward to see that all the bounds in Remark 2.6 remain valid, with constants only depending on  $\delta$ , as well as the proofs resulting from them. This reads in the following lemma, which states that all estimates of Section 2.3 remain valid at  $\underline{p}$ .
Lemma 2.14.
Assume  $1<q\leq 4$ , and  $\underline{p}$  satisfies (2.28). Then the results of Lemmas 2.7 and 2.9 still hold when replacing the left hand sides with the respective quantities at  $\underline{p}$ , with constants additionally depending on  $\delta$ . As a corollary, the results of Remarks 2.8 and 2.10 also hold with the same modifications. Furthermore, if  $q=1$  and  $\underline{p}$  satisfies (2.28), then the results of Lemma 2.11 also hold at  $\underline{p}$ .
Now we move to estimating, when fixing two edges  $e,f$ , the sum of cumulants  $\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g)$  and covariances of the form  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})$  over edges  $g\in E_{N}$  . At criticality, this is done in the proof of [25, Proposition 5.6]. The proof can directly be adapted to the case of a general environment  $\underline{p}$  satisfying  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  using Proposition 2.4 to get that if  $e,f,g$  are ordered such that  $d(e,f)$  is the smallest distance between any two of the edges, then
$\displaystyle|\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g)|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(e)}(d(e,f))\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(e)}(d(e,g))^{2}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(d(e,f))\Delta_{p_{c}}(d(e,g))^{2},$
where passing to the second line we used that  $\underline{p}$  that satisfies (2.28). One can sum this bound over edges  $g\in E_{N}$ . If  $d(e,f)=R$  one has
$\displaystyle\sum_{g\in E_{N}}|\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g)|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{r\leq R}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}+\sum_{R<r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)$
$\displaystyle\asymp\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\cdot N^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(N).$
In the above, we parametrised the position of  $g\in E_{N}$  by its distance  $r$  to  $\{e,f\}$ , which can be rewritten as
$\sum_{g\in E_{N}}|\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g)|\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}.$
(2.29)
An analogous computation gives
$\displaystyle\sum_{g\in E_{N}}|\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g)|^{2}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{r\leq R}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{4}+\sum_{R<r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{4}\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2},$
meaning that
$\sum_{g\in E_{N}}|\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g)|^{2}\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{4}\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1}.$
(2.30)
We now evaluate another sum which is useful in our proofs. Recall that for any edges  $e,f$ , one has, under the assumption (2.28), that  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\asymp\Delta_{p_{c}}(d(e,f))^{2}$ . Then one has
$\displaystyle\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\big|\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})\big|$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{d(g,e)\textrm{ or }d(g,f)\leq R}\big|\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})\big|$
$\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{d(g,e)\textrm{ and }d(g,f)>R}\big|\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})\big|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{\ell\leq R}\ell\Delta_{p_{c}}(\ell)^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}+\sum_{R<\ell\leq N}\ell\Delta_{p_{c}}(\ell)^{4}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2}.$
This can be summarized as
$\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})|\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1}.$
(2.31)
3 Near-critical random bond FK-percolation for naively centered random variables
3.1 Gaussian variables centred at  $p_{c}(q)$
3.1.1 Statement of the result and setup of the proof
Throughout this section, we fix some  $1<q\leq 4$ , and drop the dependencies in  $q$  from our notations. We start by proving Theorem 1.5 in the special case of a sequence of i.i.d. Gaussian variables whose law is given by
$\mathbf{p}_{e}\overset{(d)}{=}\mathcal{N}(p_{c}(q),\sigma_{N}^{2}),$
(3.1)
where the parameter  $\sigma_{N}$  goes to  $0$  as the size of  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$  goes to infinity. Note that the probability that a given  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  stays in the interval  $[0,1]$  is at most  $\lesssim\exp(-c\cdot\sigma_{N}^{-2})$  for some universal constant  $c>0$ . In practice,  $\sigma_{N}$  will be chosen to decay polynomially fast in  $N$ , implying, by a straightforward union bound, that all the bond parameters  $\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}$  belong to  $[0,1]$  with high probability, making the FK measures  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}$  well defined. The special role given in our analysis of the case of i.i.d. Gaussian variables is related to the so-called Skorokhod embedding theorem, which informally states that any centred random variable with regular enough integrability properties and tails can indeed be realised as some Brownian motion stopped at some well chosen stopping time. As a toy example in our analysis, we present a simplified proof of Theorem 1.5 when the random environment  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$  is given by (3.1), as it will be a first incremental step to introduce the core arguments necessary to work both for random variables satisfying either  $(\star)^{\text{A}}_{N}$  or  $(\star)^{\text{B}}_{N}$ . This reads in the following proposition.
Proposition 3.1.
Assume that the random environment  $\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}$  under  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$  is given by i.i.d Gaussians satisfying (3.1) for some uniform parameter  $\sigma_{N}$ . Then there exists  $\delta=\delta(q)>0$  and some positive constants  $c=c(q,\delta)$ ,  $O=O(q,\delta)$  such that for any  $N\geq 1$  and any  $\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}$ , one has
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\Bigg(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\sigma_{N}}\Bigg)^{2}\Bigg]\Bigg).$
Before diving into the proof, let us introduce additional notations, and highlight pieces of the strategy we use. As aforementioned, rather than directly looking at the FK measure with bonds parameters given by  $(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}$ , we introduce a time indexed continuous family of FK measures, starting at the homogeneous critical setup and ending at  $(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}$ . More precisely, for any  $t\geq 0$ , define the process  $\mathfrak{p}(t):=(\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))_{e\in E_{N}}$ , whose components are mutually independent and given by
$\mathbf{p}_{e}(t):=p_{c}(q)+B^{(e)}_{t},$
where for each  $e\in E_{N}$ ,  $t\mapsto B^{(e)}_{t}$  is a standard Brownian motion attached to the edge  $e$ . One defines the natural (completed) filtration  $\mathcal{F}^{N}_{t}:=\sigma((B^{(e)}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq t},e\in E_{N})$ , and by abuse of notation, also write  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$  for the probability measure associated to the Brownian motions. It is straightforward to see that  $\mathfrak{p}(0)=(p_{c})_{e\in E_{N}}$  and that  $t\mapsto\mathfrak{p}(t)$  is  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$ -almost surely continuous with  $\mathfrak{p}(\sigma_{N}^{2})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{=}}\mathfrak{p}$ . To prove Proposition 3.1, we will show that for  $t\lesssim\textrm{W}(N)$ , all the measures  $s\mapsto(\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s),q})_{s\leq t}$  remain within the  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  class, at least with high  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$ -probability. For the sake of notations, we will couple the evolving environment  $\mathfrak{p}(t)$  with  $\mathfrak{p}$  so that  $\mathfrak{p}(\sigma_{N}^{2})=\mathfrak{p}$ , that is to say for each  $e$ , one has  $\mathbf{p}_{e}(\sigma_{N}^{2})=\mathbf{p}_{e}$ . Our strategy enhances the ideas present in the original proof of Theorem 2.3 to our random context. More practically, this means keeping track along the time deformation of the stability of the RSW box crossing property, the mixing rates and the arm exponents everywhere in  $E_{N}$ . Some circular argument appears, as the crossing probabilities in rectangles and the arm exponents control the time dependent stochastic derivatives of the mixing rates, which control in return the time derivatives of the crossing probabilities and arm exponents. The overall interplay between those quantities will allow the FK measures to stay resembling the critical one.
Set two positive parameters  $\delta,\rho$  whose value will be fixed through the proof, and will in fact only depend on  $1<q\leq 4$ . In particular, all the constants  $\lesssim,\asymp$  will depend depend on  $\delta$  and  $\rho$  (thus on  $q$ ), except within the proof of Lemma 3.4 where the dependency will be explicited. In order to quantify the fact that the FK model with parameters  $\mathfrak{p}(t)$  deviates too much from the critical one, we introduce some breaking time  $T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , where the model no longer exhibits critical behavior, in the spirit of the deterministic breaking point  $p_{b}$  introduced in the proof of Theorem 2.3. More precisely, the random variable  $T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$  is the stopping time for the filtration  $\mathcal{F}^{N}_{t}$  corresponding to the first instant that  $\mathfrak{p}(t)$  no longer satisfies at least one of the stability conditions discussed in Section 2.5, i.e.
$T_{b}=T_{b}(\delta,\rho):=\inf\left\{t\geq 0\Bigg|\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}\not\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\cap\left(\bigcap_{\#}\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(\delta,N)\right)\cap\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\rho,N)\right\}$
where the indices  $\#$  run through  $\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\textrm{rg}},3^{\textrm{lf}}\}$ . Note that the  $\Delta$  (mixing rates) stability involves some constant  $\rho$  instead of  $\delta$ , which is a priori different, and will be fixed during the proofs. Requiring the strong box-crossing property at each scale  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  enforces (for a box of size  $1$ ) that all the edges in  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$  are open with probability between  $\delta$  and  $1-\delta$ . As a consequence, for any  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , all of the bond parameters  $\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)$  remain bounded away from  $0$  and  $1$ , making sense of the measure  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}$  up to time  $T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ . Using the very definition of  $T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , one can see Proposition 3.1 as a consequence of the fact that, with high  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$  probability, the breaking time  $T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$  is not too small. In fact, it will suffice to show that there exist constants  $\delta,\rho,c,\lesssim$  such that for all  $\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}$ ,
$\mathbf{P}\Big[T_{b}(\delta,\rho)<\sigma_{N}^{2}\Big]\lesssim\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\left(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\sigma_{N}}\right)^{2}\Bigg].$
(3.2)
Once Proposition 3.1 is related to the probability that  $T_{b}$  is not too small, the proof goes via proving that probabilities of crossing events of the form  $\phi^{0}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathfrak{p}(t),q}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]$  (similar to those introduced in Definition 1.4), mixing rates, and probabilities of arm events, do not deviate too much from their original value critical value  $\mathfrak{p}(0)$ . One (small) subtlety when applying standard FK percolation arguments relating different scales is the influence of boundary conditions on mixing (notably those on  $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}$  when considering the crossings of  $\mathcal{R}$ ). In order to sidestep this problem, one can consider some slightly more evolved crossing events, in the spirit of the properties involved in Definition  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$
Definition 3.2.
Let  $\mathcal{R}$  be a  $2$  by  $1$  rectangle of width  $R\leq N/8$  in  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$ , and let  $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}$  be the rectangle with the same center as  $\mathcal{R}$  but twice larger side lengths. Define  $\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R})$  (respectively  $\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R})$ ) to be the event that there exists a primal (respectively a dual) circuit inside the annulus  $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R}$  and separating the outer boundaries of  $\mathcal{R}$  and  $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}$ . We can then define the modified crossing events by setting, for  $\bullet\in\{h,v\}$  (see Figure 3 for an illustration)
$\begin{cases}\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{0}(\mathcal{R})&:=\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})\cap\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R}),\\
\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{\star 1}(\mathcal{R})&:=\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{\star}(\mathcal{R})\cap\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R}).\\
\end{cases}$
Figure 3: Illustration of the event  $\mathscr{C}^{0}_{h}(\mathcal{R})$ . Primal paths are depicted in full red lines and dual paths are in dashed red lines. The greyed out region is the domain  $\mathcal{D}$  introduced after Definition 3.2.
Standard conditioning and monotonicity arguments ensure that, for any  $\mathfrak{p}$  and any  $\bullet\in\{h,v\}$  one has
$\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\leq\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})|\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R})].$
Conditionally on the event  $\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R})$ , one can explore the FK clusters from  $\partial\mathcal{R}^{\prime}$  inwards, until finding a dual path circulating the annulus  $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R}$ . A piece of this path can be seen as the boundary of some domain simply connected domain  $\mathcal{D}$ , which hasn’t been explored and contains  $\mathcal{R}$  as a sub-domain (see Figure 3). The dual-connected boundary corresponds to free boundary conditions on  $\mathcal{D}$ , which implies via the domain Markov property that
$\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})|\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R})]=\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}\Big[\phi_{\mathcal{D},\mathfrak{p}}^{0}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\Big|\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R})\Big].$
As the event  $\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$  is increasing, domain monotonicity ensures that for all domains  $\mathcal{D}$  contained in  $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}$ , one has  $\phi_{\mathcal{D},\mathfrak{p}}^{0}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\leq\phi^{0}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]$ . Putting everything together gives
$\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{0}(\mathcal{R})]\leq\phi^{0}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})].$
A similar analysis for the dual model ensures that for any  $\mathfrak{p}$  and  $\bullet\in\{h,v\}$  one has
$\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{\star 1}(\mathcal{R})]\leq\phi^{1}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}^{\star}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})].$
Therefore, if one wants to check the  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  property on  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$ , it is enough to check that the both probabilities of the events  $\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{0}(\mathcal{R})$  and  $\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{\star 1}(\mathcal{R})$  remain are larger (or equal to) than  $\delta$ . In particular, one can restrict the analysis to events for the full torus measure  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}$ , not involving boundary conditions in sub-domains. Let us add that, conversely, standard RSW theory ensures that provided the measure  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}$  satisfies  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$ , then both lower bounds  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{0}(\mathcal{R})]\geq\delta^{\prime}$  and  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{\star 1}(\mathcal{R})]\geq\delta^{\prime}$  hold for some  $\delta^{\prime}>0$  only depending on  $\delta$ .
3.1.2 Proving stability of the FK measures below  $T_{b}$
One can now pass to the core of the proof, based on the following two lemmas, that evaluate how crossing probabilities, arm events and mixing rates evolve when  $\mathfrak{p}(t)$  moves from the uniform measure  $\mathfrak{p}(0)$ . All the crossing event derivatives with respect to some specific edge-weight  $p_{e}$  are recalled in Section 2.4. Hence, it remains to apply the Itô’s formula and estimate the order of magnitude of each term involved. In order to obtain  $\delta$ -dependent absolute constants, one should enforce in the reasonings presented below the possibility to chose constants only depending on  $\delta$  (and in particular  $\rho=\rho(\delta)$ ) provided  $\delta$  is small enough. In the proof of lemma 3.4, we explicitly adopt the  $\asymp_{\rho,\delta},\lesssim_{\rho,\delta}$  convention (and similarly when constants only depend on  $\delta$  or  $\rho$ ) to make the logic more transparent.
Lemma 3.3.
Assume that  $\delta$  is chosen small enough, only depending on  $1<q\leq 4$ . Then for all  $\rho>0$ , there are some positive constants  $c=c(\delta,\rho,q)>0$  and  $O_{\delta,\rho}(\cdot)$  such that if  $\sigma_{N}^{2}\leq c\cdot\textrm{W}(N)$ , one has
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall\textrm{ }0\leq s\leq\Big(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)\Big),\textrm{ }\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta,\rho}\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Bigg]\Bigg).$
Moreover, the same statement holds when replacing  $\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)$  by  $\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(2\delta,N)$  for any  $\#\in\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\textrm{rg}},3^{\textrm{lf}}\}$ .
Lemma 3.4.
Assume that  $\delta>0$  is arbitrary. Then there exists a constant  $\rho=\rho(\delta)>0$  small enough and constants  $c=c(\delta,q)>0$  and  $O_{\delta}(\cdot)$  such that if  $\sigma_{N}^{2}\leq c\cdot\textrm{W}(N)$ , one has
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall~~0\leq s\leq\Big(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)\Big),\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(2\rho,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta}\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Bigg]\Bigg).$
Let us comment on the asymmetry of the statements in these two lemmas. The stability event  $\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\rho,N)$  estimates the mixing rates  $\Delta_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}^{(e)}(R)$ , while those mixing rates are only used in computations up to multiplicative constants coming from the  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  bounds. Therefore, picking a smaller  $\delta$  in the  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  bounds worsens the bounds the mixing rates, which implies that one should in return change  $\rho$  in order show that the FK measures still belong to the  $\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\rho,N)$  class. To conclude the proof of Proposition 3.1, one needs to make a joint choice of  $\delta$  and  $\rho$ . One first picks  $\delta$  according to Lemma 3.3, and then selects  $\rho$  according to Lemma 3.4 according to  $\delta$ . We now pass to the proof of the aforementioned lemmas, starting with Lemma 3.3, using the Itô formula to bound stochastic derivatives in the random environment.
Proof of Lemma 3.3.
Let  $\mathcal{S}$  be any event defined on  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$ . Since the standard Brownian motions  $\big((B^{(e)}_{t})_{t\geq 0}\big)_{e\in E_{N}}$  are i.i.d , one can apply the Itô lemma which reads as
$\mathrm{d}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{S}]=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}\bigg\rvert_{\underline{p}=\mathfrak{p}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p}}[\mathcal{S}]\right)\mathrm{d}B^{(e)}_{t}+\frac{1}{2}\Bigg(\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\left(\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{e}^{2}}\bigg\rvert_{\underline{p}=\mathfrak{p}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p}}[\mathcal{S}]\right)\Bigg)\mathrm{d}t,$
where the  $\mathrm{d}$  operator corresponds to the standard stochastic differentiation. Plugging the explicit formulae obtained in Proposition 2.13 one gets
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{S}]$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}B^{(e)}_{t}$
$\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]\right)\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}t.$
We are going to evaluate the order of magnitude of the two previous lines for times  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$  for the special case of the events
$\mathcal{S}=\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$  or  $\mathcal{S}=\mathscr{C}^{\star 1}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$ . One of the takeaway points of [25] is the possibility, at and near criticality, to express event covariances and edge-influences only using mixing rates  $\Delta$ . Below the breaking time  $T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , all the mixing rates remain comparable up to constant to the critical ones  $\Delta_{p_{c}}$ , whose analysis in [25] was recalled in Section 2.5. We only work out the details when  $\mathcal{S}=\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$ , the case  $\mathcal{S}=\mathscr{C}^{\star 1}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$  can be treated similarly. The cases  $\bullet=h$  and  $\bullet=v$  are exactly identical so we just write  $\bullet$  for the proof.
Step 0: Canonical decomposition of the semimartingale.
Fix a  $2$  by  $1$  rectangle  $\mathcal{R}\in\mathbb{T}_{N}$  of width  $R\leq 8$ . Using the classical semimartingale decomposition, one can write  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]=M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}+A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$  where  $M^{\mathcal{R}}$  is a local martingale started at  $0$  and  $A^{\mathcal{R}}$  is an adapted finite variation process, whose exact expression are given by
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}B^{(e)}_{t},$
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]\right)\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}t.$
Step 1: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$ .
We are going to first evaluate  $A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$  using the critical mixing rates  $\Delta_{p_{c}}$ . Recall that provided  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , the  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  property applied to rectangles of size  $2\times 1$  and  $1\times 2$  ensures that coupling constants  $\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)$  are bounded away from  $0$  and  $1$ . This ensures in particular that there exists a constant  $O(1)$ , only depending on  $\delta$  chosen small enough such that
$\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))^{2}}=O_{\delta}(1),\quad\left(1-\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t),q}[\omega_{e}]\right)=O_{\delta}(1).$
(3.3)
One can therefore write the crude estimate
$\displaystyle\Bigg|\frac{\mathrm{d}A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Bigg|$
$\displaystyle=\Bigg|\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t),q}[\omega_{e}]\right)\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\Bigg|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim_{\delta}\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e}).$
Still for  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , the measure  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t),q}$  belongs to all of the required stability events from Section 2.5. Therefore, one may use equation (2.22), which holds due to Lemma 2.14 to get
$\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}.$
(3.4)
Note that (2.22) is in principle written for the event  $\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$  and not  $\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$ . Still, the exact same proof holds for this modified crossing event, except one has to take care of both the corners of  $\mathcal{R}$  and  $\mathcal{R}^{\prime}$ . Integrating in time  $t$  shows that  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$  one has
$|A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}-A^{\mathcal{R}}_{0}|\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}\frac{t}{\textrm{W}(N)}.$
(3.5)
Step 2: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$ .
We now evaluate the the rate of growth of local martingale part  $M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$ . Itô’s formula gives the following expression for its bracket:
$\mathrm{d}\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\left(\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}\right)\mathrm{d}t.$
Using again (3.3), one deduces that
$\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\lesssim_{\delta}\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}.$
(3.6)
Once again, for  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , there exist some  $c=c(q)>0$  such that
$\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}\Xi(N)^{-1}\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}N^{-c}\textrm{W}(N)^{-1},$
where the first inequality comes from (2.24) and the second one from Lemma 2.12. Integrating this equation up to some time  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$  gives
$\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}N^{-c}\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}\cdot t.$
(3.7)
Step 3: Concluding via large deviations for  $M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$ .
We are now in position to conclude. Informally speaking, if there is an instant  $t\ll\sigma_{N}^{2}$  such that  ${\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}\not\in\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)}$ , then there is at least one  $2$  by  $1$  rectangle  $\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}$  such that the local martingale  $M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$  achieved a much greater value than what its bracket should allow. Let us clarify the reasoning, highlighting where it becomes crucial to have  $\delta$  small enough.
(1)
First pick  $\delta>0$  small enough and uniform in  $N$  such that  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p_{c}}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\geq 4\delta$  for all  $2$  by  $1$  rectangles  $\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}$ . Crucially, this  $\delta$  only depends on  $q$ .
(2)
Using (3.5), one gets that there is a constant  $C=C(\delta,\rho)>0$  such that for any  $2$  by  $1$  rectangle  $\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}$  and any  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$  one has
$|A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}-A^{\mathcal{R}}_{0}|\leq\frac{C\cdot t}{\textrm{W}(N)}\leq\frac{C\cdot\sigma_{N}^{2}}{\textrm{W}(N)}$
Fixing  $c_{1}:=\sqrt{\frac{\delta}{C}}$ , this implies that for  $\sigma_{N}\leq c_{1}\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}$ , one has (deterministically)
$|A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}-A^{\mathcal{R}}_{0}|\leq\delta$
(3)
Assuming that the event  $\Big\{\exists\textrm{ }0\leq s\leq\Big(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)\Big),\textrm{ }\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\not\in\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)\Big\}$  holds, there exists (if  $\sigma_{N}\leq c_{1}\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}$ ) at least one  $2$  by  $1$  rectangle  $\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}$  such that
$\sup_{0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)}\Big|\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]-\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p_{c}}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\Big|>2\delta.$
(3.8)
Combining with the previous inequalities for that specific rectangle  $\mathcal{R}$  implies that provided  $\sigma_{N}\leq c_{1}\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}$  one has
$\sup_{0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)}\Big|M^{\mathcal{R}}_{s}\Big|>\delta$
(4)
One can now use standard large deviation estimates for local martingales. Using (3.7), there exists some constant  $c=c(q,\delta)>0$  such that for any  $2$  by  $1$  rectangle  $\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}$  and any  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$  one has
$\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}\leq c^{-1}N^{-c}\frac{t}{\textrm{W}(N)}\leq c^{-1}N^{-c}\frac{\sigma_{N}^{2}}{\textrm{W}(N)}.$
(3.9)
Using standard large deviation principles, one can control the supremum and the infimum of a local martingale started at  $0$  via its bracket, which reads (choosing if needed  $c$  smaller than its value in (3.9)) as
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[\sup_{0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)}|M^{\mathcal{R}}_{s}|>\delta\right]\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Bigg].$
Applying the previous remark to each of the  $O(N^{3})$   $2$  by  $1$  rectangles inside  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$ , a union bound ensures that
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[\inf_{\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}}\inf_{\bullet=h,v}\inf_{0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]<2\delta\right]\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}N^{3}\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Bigg].$
The complement of the event inside  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$  in the above equation is the event that for any  $0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$  and any  $2$  by  $1$  rectangle  $\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}$ , the probability of any primal crossing  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]$  is at least  $2\delta$ . Doing the same reasoning for dual crossings and replacing  $c$  by  $\frac{c}{2}$  concludes the proof.
Adapting the proof for arm events.
When proving the stability of the arm events  $\mathcal{A}^{(e)}_{\#}(R)$ , one can run almost verbatim the proof made for the crossing event  $\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$ , replacing (2.22) and (2.24) by respectively
(2.25) and (2.26). In this case, the probabilities of arm events  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{A}^{(e)}_{\#}(R)]$  are not bounded away from  $0$  and  $1$  uniformly in  $N$ , so one needs to keep track of the additional pre-factors  $\pi_{\#,p_{c}}(R)$  that appear in front of the stochastic derivatives, exactly as in Remark 2.10.
∎
We prove now Lemma 3.4 with very similar methods, using a slightly more delicate strategy due when controlling the covariances between multiple edges.
Proof of lemma 3.4.
We proceed here similarly to the proof of Theorem 2.3, where the stability of the mixing rates  $\Delta_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}$  is derived from the stability of the edge-covariances of the form  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$ . A priori, as long as  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , the covariances  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$  are uniformly comparable with  $\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$ , but with some constants depending on  $\rho$  and  $\delta$ . The goal of this proof is to carefully underline the fact that  $\rho$  is chosen only depending on  $\delta$ .
Step 0: Canonical decomposition of the semimartingale
Fix two edges  $e,f\in E_{N}$  at distance  $R$  from each other. One can use the identities of Proposition 2.13 together with the Ito formula to write  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})=M^{e,f}_{t}+A^{e,f}_{t}$  where
$M^{e,f}$  is a local martingale started at  $0$  and  $A^{e,f}$  is a bounded variation process adapted to filtration  $\mathcal{F}^{N}_{s}$ , whose respective expressions are given by
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}M_{t}^{e,f}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\Bigg(\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{g}}\bigg\rvert_{\underline{p}=\mathfrak{p}(t)}\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\Bigg)\mathrm{d}B^{(g)}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\Bigg(\frac{1}{\textbf{p}_{g}(t)(1-\textbf{p}_{g}(t))}\kappa^{\mathfrak{p}(t)}_{3}(e,f,g)\Bigg)\mathrm{d}B^{(g)}_{t},$
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}A_{t}^{e,f}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\Bigg(\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{g}^{2}}\bigg\rvert_{\underline{p}=\mathfrak{p}(t)}\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\Bigg)\mathrm{d}t$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\textbf{p}_{g}(t)(1-\textbf{p}_{g}(t))^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{\textbf{p}_{g}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{g}]\right)\kappa_{3}^{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(e,f,g)\mathrm{d}t$
$\displaystyle\quad-\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\textbf{p}_{g}(t)^{2}(1-\textbf{p}_{g}(t))^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})\mathrm{d}t.$
Step 1: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $A^{e,f}_{t}$ .
Using again (3.3) (which states that all the bonds  $\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)$  are bounded away from  $0$  and  $1$ ) one has for  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , the triangular inequality provides the upper bound
$\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}A^{e,f}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\lesssim_{\delta}\sum_{g\in E_{N}}|\kappa_{3}^{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(e,f,g)|+\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g}).$
(3.10)
Step 1.1: Estimating the  $\kappa_{3}^{\mathfrak{p}(t)}$  terms in (3.10).
As in the proof of Lemma 3.3, for  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , we may use the results of Section 2.5, with constants depending on both  $\delta$  and  $\rho$ . Using equation (2.29) and recalling that  $d(e,f)=R$ , one has
$\sum_{g\in E_{N}}|\kappa_{3}^{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(e,f,g)|\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}.$
Step 1.2: Estimating the  $\textrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}$  terms in (3.10).
Let us now estimate the terms of involved in the  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})$  sum. This is simply the computation made in Section 2.5 and equation (2.31) gives
$\sum_{g\in E_{N}}|\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})|\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1}$
Step 1.3: Concluding on the estimate of  $\frac{\mathrm{d}A^{e,f}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}$ .
Due to Lemma 2.12, the term given by the sum of products of covariances is polynomially smaller than the estimate for the sum of the  $\kappa_{3}^{\mathfrak{p}(t)}$  terms. Therefore, one may write
$\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}A^{e,f}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}.$
Step 2: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $M^{e,f}_{t}$ .
We can again evaluate the order of magnitude of the local martingale  $M^{e,f}_{t}$  via its bracket  $\langle M^{e,f}\rangle_{t}$ . As long as  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , one can (2.30) from Section 2.5 and deduce that
$\displaystyle\Bigg|\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle M^{e,f}\rangle_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Bigg|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim_{\delta}\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\Big(\kappa_{3}^{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(e,f,g)\Big)^{2}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{4}\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1}.$
Finally, Lemma 2.12 ensures the existence of  $c=c(q)>0$  such that
$\forall\ 0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho),\quad\Bigg|\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle M^{e,f}\rangle_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Bigg|\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{4}N^{-c}\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}.$
Step 3: Proving that covariances remain stable via large deviations of  $M^{e,f}_{t}$ .
One can now repeat exactly the large deviation arguments within Step 3 the proof of Lemma 3.3 (with additional  $\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)$  pre-factors) and deduce that for any  $\varepsilon>0$ , there exist some constants  $c_{1}=c_{1}(\delta,\rho,\varepsilon,q)>0$  and  $c_{2}=c_{2}(\delta,\rho,\varepsilon,q)>0$  such that as long  $\sigma_{N}^{2}\leq c_{2}\cdot\textrm{W}(N)$  one has
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\exists\ e,f\in E_{N},\exists\ 0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho),\frac{\Big|\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(s)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})-\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\Big|}{\Delta_{p_{c}}(d(e,f))^{2}}>\varepsilon\Bigg]\\
\lesssim_{\delta}\exp\Bigg[-c_{1}N^{c_{1}}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Bigg].$
For the critical measure, one has  $\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\asymp\Delta_{p_{c}}(d(e,f))^{2}$  uniformly in  $e,f\in E_{N}$ . Therefore, there exists a constant  $C=C(q)>0$  such that
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\exists\ e,f\in E_{N},\exists\ 0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho),\Bigg|\frac{\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(s)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})}{\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})}-1\Bigg|>C\varepsilon\Bigg]\\
\lesssim_{\delta,\rho}\exp\Bigg[-c_{1}N^{c_{1}}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Bigg].$
One can now fix  $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(q)$  smaller than  $\frac{1}{2C}$  such that the event
$\Bigg\{\forall\ e,f\in E_{N},\forall\ 0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho),\Bigg|\frac{\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(s)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})}{\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})}-1\Bigg|\leq\frac{1}{2}\Bigg\}$
(3.11)
happens with high probability assuming  $\sigma_{N}^{2}\leq c_{2}\cdot\textrm{W}(N)$ . Under this event, one has  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(s)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\asymp\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$  uniformly in  $e,f\in E_{N}$ , for some universal constant  $\asymp$  (i.e. not depending on  $\delta,\rho$ ).
Step 4: Concluding that mixing rates remain stable.
Fix an edge  $e\in\mathbb{T}_{N}$  and  $R\leq N$ . Let  $g$  be an edge at distance  $R$  from  $e$ , and  $f$  an edge approximating the midpoint of the shortest segment from  $e$  to  $g$ . As long as  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , the measure  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}$  belongs to  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$ , therefore one can write
$\frac{\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})}{\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})}\asymp_{\delta}\frac{\Delta^{(e)}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(R/2)\Delta^{(f)}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(R/2)\Delta^{(e)}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(R)\Delta^{(g)}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(R)}{\Delta^{(f)}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(R/2)\Delta^{(g)}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(R/2)}\asymp_{\delta}\Delta^{(e)}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(R)^{2}.$
Therefore, on the event (3.11), which happens with a probability greater than
$1-O_{\delta,\rho}\Big(\exp\Big[-c_{1}N^{c_{1}}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Big]\Big)$ ), one can reconstruct (up to constants) the mixing rates via the the covariances using the formula
$\Delta^{(e)}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(R)\asymp_{\delta}\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})}{\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})}}.$
This last estimate doesn’t depend on  $\rho$ , as it is only tied to the  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  property as recalled in the first item of Proposition 2.4. Still on the event (3.11), one has
$\Delta^{(e)}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(R)\asymp_{\delta}\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})}{\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})}}\asymp_{\delta}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R).$
Taking  $\rho=\rho(\delta)$  to be half of the implicit  $\asymp_{\delta}$  constant in the previous equation (meaning that the ratio between critical and random mixing rates remains in  $[2\rho,1/2\rho]$ ), one can conclude that with probability greater than  $1-O_{\delta,\rho}\Big(\exp\Big[-c_{1}N^{c_{1}}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Big]\Big)$ , all of the measures  $(\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)})_{0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)}$  belong to  $\textrm{Stab}(2\rho(\delta),N)$ . This concludes the proof.
∎
One can now combine the two previous lemmas to prove Proposition 3.1.
Proof of Proposition 3.1.
Choose first  $\delta$  small enough according to Lemma 3.3 and then  ${\rho=\rho(\delta)>0}$  according to Lemma 3.4. There exist  $c>0$  such that
$\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall\,0\leq s\leq\big(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)\big),\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)\cap\Big(\bigcap_{\#}\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(2\delta,N)\Big)\cap\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(2\rho,N)\Bigg]$
$\displaystyle\geq 1-O_{\delta}\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Bigg]\Bigg).$
The Brownian trajectories are  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$ -almost surely time continuous, which implies the same statement for crossing probabilities and mixing rates. For each realization of the event
$\Bigg\{\forall~0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho),~\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)\cap\Big(\bigcap_{\#}\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(2\delta,N)\Big)\cap\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(2\rho,N)\Bigg\},$
there exists a (realization dependent)  $\varepsilon>0$  such that
$\forall~0\leq s\leq\big(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)\big)+\varepsilon,\quad\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\cap\left(\bigcap_{\#}\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(\delta,N)\right)\cap\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\rho,N).$
On that event, one has  $T_{b}(\delta,\rho)>(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho))+\varepsilon$ , hence  $\sigma_{N}^{2}<T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ . This reads as
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Big[T_{b}(\delta,\rho)<\sigma_{N}^{2}\Big]\lesssim_{\delta}\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Bigg],$
which allows to conclude via the reformulation (3.2) of Proposition 3.1.
∎
3.2 General random variables satisfying  $(\star)^{\textmd{A}}_{N}$
In Section 3.1, we proved Theorem 1.5 in the specific case when the random bond parameters are independent Gaussians with a common variance. The role of the present section is to explain how one can extend the proof of this result to a sequence of variables  $(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}$  satisfying the condition  $(\star)^{\text{A}}_{N}$ . Recall that at each edge  $e\in E_{N}$ , the random variable  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  has standard deviation  $\sigma_{e}:=\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c})^{2}]^{1/2}$ . Ideally, one would like to apply exactly the same reasoning as the Gaussian case, by continuously moving the bond parameters from the uniform critical parameter  $p_{c}(q)$  towards  $\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e}$  via some continuous process  $\mathfrak{p}(t)=(\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))_{e\in E_{N}}$ . In fact, we would like this continuous process to resemble independent Brownian motions, allowing us to repeat the technology developed in Section 3.1. This ideal setup can in fact be achieved by the famous Skorokhod embedding theorem, that allows to rewrite any reasonable centred random variable as some Brownian motion stopped appropriately. This reads in the following theorem.
Theorem 3.5 (Skorokhod embedding theorem).
Let  $X$  be a centred real value random variable with a finite second moment. Let  $(B_{t})_{t\geq 0}$  a standard Brownian motion for some (completed) filtration  $(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ . Then there exist some stopping time  $T$  for the filtration  $(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$  such that
$\begin{array}[]{rcl}B_{T}&\overset{(d)}{=}&X,\\
\mathbb{E}[T]&=&\mathbb{E}[X^{2}].\end{array}$
We now explain how to implement the Skorokhod embedding theorem in the context of the random bond measure  $\mathfrak{p}$ . There exist a sequence of independent Brownian motions  $\big((B_{t}^{(e)})_{t\geq 0}\big)_{e\in E_{N}}$  for some probability measure  $\mathbb{P}$  and a sequence of associated stopping times  $\big(T^{(e)}\big)_{e\in E_{N}}$  for the Brownian motions  $\big((B_{t}^{(e)})_{t\geq 0}\big)_{e\in E_{N}}$ , such that for each edge  $e\in E_{N}$ , the variable  $p_{c}+B^{(e)}_{T^{(e)}}$  has the law of  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$ . One can set
$\mathbf{p}_{e}(t):=p_{c}(q)+B^{(e)}_{t\wedge T^{(e)}}.$
(3.12)
The stopping times  $T^{(e)}$  coming from Skorokhod’s embedding theorem are almost surely finite, which implies that almost surely (with respect to the randomness of the Brownian motions) one has  $\mathbf{p}_{e}(\infty)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{=}}\mathbf{p}_{e}$ . To simplify readability, couple the process  $\mathfrak{p}(t)$  to the random environment  $\mathfrak{p}$  so that this equality in distribution as an equality.
The stopping times given by the Skorokhod embedding theorem are a priori not unique, and we present here a construction that gives a stopping time with good tails estimates. The following technical lemma is proven in the Appendix via Lemma B.1.
Lemma 3.6.
Let  $X$  be a random variable with stretched exponential tails
$\mathbb{P}[X>t]\lesssim\exp(-ct^{\gamma})$
for some positive constants  $\lesssim,c,\gamma$ . Let  $(B_{t})_{t\geq 0}$  be a standard Brownian motion for the filtration  $(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ . Then there exists a stopping time  $T$ , for the filtration  $(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ , that satisfies the Skorokhod embedding Theorem and such that
$\mathbb{P}[T>t]\lesssim\exp\left(-c^{\prime}t^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\right)$
for some positive constants  $\lesssim,c^{\prime}$  only depending on  $c$  and  $\gamma$ .
Applying this result to the random variables  $\frac{\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q)}{\sigma_{e}}$  with  $\gamma=1$  (using the third condition in the definition of  $(\star)^{\text{A}}_{N}$  and the Brownian scaling), there exists a stopping time  $T^{(e)}$  such that
$\mathbb{P}[T^{(e)}>t]\lesssim\exp\left[-c^{\prime}\left(\frac{t}{\sigma_{e}^{2}}\right)^{1/3}\right],$
where all constants involved are uniform in  $N$  and  $e\in E_{N}$ . Recall that we denoted  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}:=\max_{e\in E_{N}}\sigma_{e}$ . Therefore, as for any  $e\in E_{N}$  one has  $\sigma_{e}\leq\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}$ , and so uniformly in  $e\in E_{N}$  and  $t>0$ ,
$\mathbb{P}\big[T^{(e)}/\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}>t\big]\lesssim\exp\left[-c^{\prime}t^{1/3}\right].$
We now adapt the proof of Section 3.1, keeping the same notations, replacing the Brownian motions  $\mathfrak{p}(t)$  by the Brownian motions stopped at  $T^{(e)}$  defined in (3.12). In this new setting,  $\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{p}(\infty)$ , and we want to show that the event  $\big\{T_{b}=\infty\big\}$  happens with high  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$ -probability. We start by recalling the following elementary lemma, whose proof is given in the Appendix B.3.
Lemma 3.7.
Fix a sequence of positive numbers  $(a_{i})_{i\leq M}$  with  $m=\max_{i\leq M}a_{i}$  and  $S=\sum_{i\leq M}a_{i}$ . Let  $(T_{i})_{i\leq M}$  be a collection of positive random variables with uniform stretched exponential tails for some  $0<\gamma<1$
$\mathbb{P}[T_{i}>t]\lesssim\exp\Big[-ct^{\gamma}\Big].$
Then there exist positive constants  $C=C(c,\gamma)$  and  $\tilde{c}=\tilde{c}(c,\gamma)>0$  such that uniformly in  $t>C\cdot S$ , one has
$\mathbb{P}\Bigg[\sum_{i\leq M}a_{i}T_{i}>t\Bigg]\lesssim\exp\Big[-\tilde{c}\cdot\Big(\frac{t}{m}\Big)^{\gamma}\Big].$
In the spirit of the previous section, we will prove a pair of lemmas that show that, with high probability, the main features of the critical measure remain stable for a large enough amount of time.
Lemma 3.8.
Assume that  $\delta>0$  is chosen small enough, only depending on  $1<q\leq 4$ . Then for all  $\rho>0$ , there are some positive constants  $c=c(\delta,\rho,q)>0$  and  $O_{\delta,\rho}(\cdot)$  such that if  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}\leq c\cdot\textrm{W}(N)$ , one has
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall\textrm{ }0\leq s\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho),\textrm{ }\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta,\rho}\left(\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\left(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\Bigg]\right).$
Moreover, the same statement holds when replacing  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  by  $\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(2\delta,N)$  for any  $\#\in\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\text{rg}},3^{\text{lf}}\}$ .
Lemma 3.9.
Assume that  $\delta>0$  is arbitrary. Then there  $\rho=\rho(\delta)>0$  small enough and constants  $c=c(\delta,q)>0$  and  $O_{\delta}(\cdot)$  such that if  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}\leq c\cdot\textrm{W}(N)$ , one has
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall\ 0\leq s\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho),\ \phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(2\rho,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta}\left(\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\left(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\Bigg]\right).$
The proofs of these lemmas and how they allow to deduce Theorem 1.5 are very similar to the previous section. Therefore, we only sketch the proof of Lemma 3.8 for crossing events to illustrate how the control of the tails for the spotting times recalled in Lemma 3.7 allows to control the probability of crossing events.
Sketch of the proof of Lemma 3.8 for crossing events.
Let  $\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}$  be a  $2$  by  $1$  rectangle of width  $R\leq N/8$ , and apply Itô’s formula to the process  $t\mapsto\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]$ .
Step 0: Canonical decomposition of the semimartingale
One can make the decomposition  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]=M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}+A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$  where  $M^{\mathcal{R}}$  is a local martingale started at  $0$  and  $A^{\mathcal{R}}$  is an adapted finite variation process, given by
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\mathbbm{1}(t\leq T^{(e)})\mathrm{d}B^{(e)}_{t},$
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]\right)\mathbbm{1}(t\leq T^{(e)})\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}t.$
Step 1: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$
Similarly to the previous section one can write for all  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ ,
$\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\lesssim\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\mathbbm{1}(t\leq T^{(e)}).$
Still assuming that  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$ , one can apply Lemma 2.14 which implies that each  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})$  term can be estimated via Lemma 2.7 (more precisely working for crossing events of the form  $\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$  as at the end of the proof of Step 1 of Lemma 3.3). Set
$\alpha(\mathcal{R},e):=\begin{cases}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R,\ell)\Delta_{p_{c}}(\ell)&\text{if }\textrm{dist}(e,\mathcal{R})=\ell\geq R\\
\Delta_{p_{c}}(n)&\text{if the distance from }e\text{ to the corners of }\mathcal{R}\text{ is }n\lesssim R.\end{cases}$
One can then apply Lemma 2.7, which implies that for  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}$ , one has the upper bound  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\lesssim\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)$ . Integrating this information for  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}$  gives
$\left|A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}-A^{\mathcal{R}}_{0}\right|\lesssim\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)(t\wedge T^{(e)})\leq\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)T^{(e)}$
One can also notice that (2.22) ensures that  $\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)\lesssim\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}$ , while one can crudely bound  $\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)\lesssim 1$ . We are in position to apply Lemma 3.7 to the family of variables  $\big(T^{(e)}/\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}\big)_{e\in E_{N}}$ , which shows the existence of universal constants  $C,\tilde{c},c_{1}$  such that if  $c_{1}\delta/\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}\geq C\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}$ , one has
$\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{N}\Big[\exists\ 0\leq t\leq T_{b},\quad\left|A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}-A^{\mathcal{R}}_{0}\right|>\delta\Big]$
$\displaystyle\leq\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)T^{(e)}\geq c_{1}\delta\right]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left[-\tilde{c}\left(\frac{c_{1}\delta}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}}\right)^{1/3}\right].$
Fix  $c_{2}:=c_{1}\delta/C$  and  $c_{3}:=\frac{1}{2}\tilde{c}c_{1}^{1/3}\delta^{1/3}$ . Taking the union bound over the  $O(N^{3})$   $2$  by  $1$  rectangles  $\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}$ , one sees that provided  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}\leq c_{2}\textrm{W}(N)$ , one has
$\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{N}\Big[\exists\ \mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N},\exists\ 0\leq t\leq T_{b},\quad\left|A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}-A^{\mathcal{R}}_{0}\right|>\delta\Big]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim N^{3}\exp\left[-2c_{3}\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-2/3}\right]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left[-c_{3}\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-2/3}\right].$
where in the last line we used that  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}\lesssim\textrm{W}(N)$  decays polynomially fast in  $N$ . Note that if  $c>0$  is small enough, this probability is much smaller than the one in the statement of the lemma.
In the present context,
$\left|A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}-A^{\mathcal{R}}_{0}\right|$  is not deterministically bounded from above. Instead, the present reasoning shows that, only with very low probability, the quantity  $\left|A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}-A^{\mathcal{R}}_{0}\right|$  is large, allowing to easily adapt the previous arguments.
Step 2: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $M_{t}^{\mathcal{R}}$ .
One has for  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}$
$\displaystyle\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}\mathbbm{1}(t\leq T^{(e)})$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)^{2}\mathbbm{1}(t\leq T^{(e)}).$
Integrating the above one gets for  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}$
$\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}\lesssim\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)^{2}(t\wedge T^{(e)})\leq\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)^{2}T^{(e)}.$
Using (2.24) gives
$\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)^{2}\lesssim\Xi(N)^{-1}.$
One can now apply Lemma 3.7 to the random variables  $T^{(e)}/\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}$  with the trivial bound that each  $\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)^{2}$  is smaller than  $\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)^{2}$ , which provides the existence of positive constants  $C,\tilde{c},c_{1}$  such that if  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\Xi(N)^{-1/4}\Big/\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}\geq C\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1}$  one has
$\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{T_{b}}>\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\Xi(N)^{-1/4}\right]$
$\displaystyle\leq\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha(\mathcal{R},e)^{2}T^{(e)}\geq c_{1}\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\Xi(N)^{-1/4}\right]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left[-2\tilde{c}\left(\frac{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\Xi(N)^{-1/4}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}\Xi(N)^{-1}}\right)^{1/3}\right]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left[-2\tilde{c}N^{\tilde{c}}\left(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\right],$
where in the last line, we used Lemma 2.12, potentially changing the constant  $\tilde{c}$ .
Note that the condition on  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}$ , required to apply Lemma 3.7, is equivalent to  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}\leq C^{-2/3}\cdot\Xi(N)^{1/2}$ , which, by Lemma 2.12, is satisfied for  $N$  large enough as long as  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}\lesssim\textrm{W}(N)$ . The union bound on  $\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}$  ensures that if  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}\lesssim\textrm{W}(N)$ , one has
$\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[\exists\ \mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N},\quad\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{T_{b}}>\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\Xi(N)^{-1/4}\right]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim N^{3}\exp\left[-2\tilde{c}N^{\tilde{c}}\left(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\right]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left[-\tilde{c}N^{\tilde{c}}\left(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\right].$
Concluding via large deviation estimates
Define the event
$G:=\Big\{\forall\,\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N},\,\forall\,0\leq t\leq T_{b},\;|A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}-A^{\mathcal{R}}_{0}|\leq\delta\Big\}\bigcap\left\{\forall\,\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N},\;\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{T_{b}}\leq\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\Xi(N)^{-1/4}\right\},$
which happens with probability at least  $1-O\left(\exp\left[-\tilde{c}N^{\tilde{c}}\left(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\right]\right)$ . On this event, one can use large deviation estimates for local martingales and Lemma 2.12, which ensure the existence of some  $c>0$  small enough such that
$\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[G\bigcap\Big\{\sup_{\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}}\sup_{0\leq s\leq T_{b}}|M^{\mathcal{R}}_{s}|>\delta\Big\}\right]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim N^{3}\exp\left[-2c\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-1/2}\Xi(N)^{1/4}\right]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left[-cN^{c}\left(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\right].$
One may now conclude as in the proof of Proposition 3.1.
∎
4 Random variables naturally centred near  $p_{c}(q)$
In the previous section we perturbed the environment from the critical one, using variables which were naively centred around the critical point, requiring that the expected value of the random bond parameter was  $p_{c}(q)$ . The toy example for the analysis was the use of some Brownian motions up to some small time  $t\ll 1$ , whose typical order of magnitude is  $\sqrt{t}$ . Looking more carefully, this approach might look too naive, as one wants a near-critical random environment which remains in the critical phase, therefore neither favouring too much much the primal or the dual model. As our random bond parametrisation is not naturally centred around  $p_{c}$  from the perspective of self-duality, it is tempting to add a drift correction to the Brownian motions in order to preserve self-duality of the expected random environment up to its second moment. Note that in the natural isoradial parametrisation of the FK model (see e.g. [24]), this drift would vanish. To each of the Brownian motions, we add a drift  $-\mu(q)\cdot t$ , as a natural second order expansion for a random process near  $0$ . In the present section, the critical window in random environment will be expressed via the quantity  $\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)=\textrm{W}(N)(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4})^{-1/2}$ . As CLE computations assert that the mixing rate  $\iota$  is larger than  $\frac{1}{2}$  (with equality only at  $q=4$ ), the multiplicative correction to  $\textrm{W}(N)$  is conjectured to be of constant order for  $1<q<4$  and sub-polynomial for  $q=4$ , and so the results should be interpreted as involving the normal critical window  $\textrm{W}(N)$  instead of  $\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)$ .
4.1 The special case of Gaussian variables
4.1.1 Statement of the result and setup of the proof
In this section, we prove an analog of Theorem 1.6 in the special case of a sequence of i.i.d. Gaussian variables whose law is given by
$\mathbf{p}_{e}\overset{(d)}{=}\mathcal{N}(p_{c}(q)-\mu(q)\sigma_{N},\sigma_{N}^{2}),$
(4.1)
where the parameter  $\sigma_{N}$  goes to  $0$  as the size of  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$  goes to infinity, which ensures once again that with high probability (i.e. not worsening all the other estimates involved), all the edge weights  $\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}$  remain in  $(0,1)$ . We use once again i.i.d. Gaussian variables aiming to generalise afterwards by applying Skorohod’s embedding theorem. We modify the i.i.d. Brownian motions from the previous section by adding a linear drift at each edge. Compared to the proof of Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4, adding some well chosen drift allows us to lower (with high probability) the order of magnitude of the finite variation processes of the form  $A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$  and  $A^{e,f}_{t}$ , which were identified as being the dominant terms in the respective Itô derivatives. As it will be discussed in Section 4.3, the conceptual reason to subtract that exact drift  $t\mapsto\mu(q)t$  is to construct a random environment under  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$  which is on average almost self-dual for its first two moments as in scenario  $(\star)_{N}^{\text{B}}$ . We keep the notations of Section 4.1 and skip most details in the proofs that exactly match those of the previous section. This time, we prove a simplified version of Theorem 1.6 when  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$  is given (4.1). Note that Lemma 2.12 ensures that the following result represents a strict improvement of the results obtained in Section 3, as there exists  $c>0$ , depending on  $q$ , such that
$\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\gtrsim\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}N^{c}$ .
Proposition 4.1.
Fix  $1<q\leq 4$ . Assume that the random environment  $(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}$  under  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$  is given by i.i.d Gaussian satisfying (4.1) for some uniform parameter  $\sigma_{N}$ . Then there exists some  $\delta=\delta(q)>0$  and some constant  $c=c(\delta,q)>0$  such that for any  $N\geq 1$  and  $\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\log(N)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Bigg]>1-O\left(\exp\Bigg[-c\cdot\Bigg(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\sigma_{N}}\Bigg)^{2}\Bigg]\right).$
In this section, for  $t\geq 0$ , one can define the stochastic process  $\mathfrak{p}(t):=(\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))_{e\in E_{N}}$ , formed of independent components given by
$\mathbf{p}_{e}(t):=p_{c}(q)+B^{(e)}_{t}-\mu(q)t,$
where  $t\mapsto B^{(e)}_{t}$  is a standard Brownian motion attached to the edge  $e$  and we recall the expression  $\mu(q)=\frac{q-1}{2\sqrt{q}}$ . Again  $\mathfrak{p}(0)=(p_{c})_{e\in E_{N}}$  while  $t\mapsto\mathfrak{p}(t)$  is almost surely continuous and evolves towards the random process  $\mathfrak{p}(\sigma_{N}^{2})\overset{(d)}{=}(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in\mathbb{T}_{N}}$ . In that case, Proposition 4.1 reads that if  $t\lesssim\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{2/3}\log(N)^{-1}$ , then, with high probability, all the measures  $s\mapsto(\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)})_{s\leq t}$  remain within the  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  class. We keep the  $\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(\delta,N),\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\rho,N)$  and  $T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$  notations of the previous sections. Once again, the building block to prove Proposition 4.1 is a generalisation of Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4.
Consider an event  $\mathcal{S}$  and apply the Itô formula to  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{S}]$  with this new process  $\mathfrak{p}(t)$ . A straightforward computation shows that
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{S}]$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}B^{(e)}_{t}$
$\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}t$
where the  $\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)$  is some process which can be computed using the expressions for  $\mu(q)$  and  $p_{c}(q)$ , and is given explicitely by
$\mathbf{r}_{e}(t):=\frac{2p_{c}-1}{2p_{c}(1-p_{c})}-\frac{2\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)-1}{2\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\left(1+\frac{1-2\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]}{2\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)}\right).$
(4.2)
If one wants to apply verbatim the reasoning of the previous section, one can brutally bound  $\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)$  by a constant to obtain the same result. However, the drift is chosen specifically such that for any edge  $e$ ,  $\mathbf{r}_{e}(0)=0$ . This hints that one can obtain some better bound than constant for  $\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)$  near  $t=0$ , which will in fact be of order  $\sqrt{t}$ . This lowers the value of all the finite variation processes involved in the semi-martingale decompositions and allows us to run the stochastic processes (here with drift) for a longer amount of time while remaining within the critical phase (in the sense of Section 2.5).
4.1.2 A preliminary estimate on  $\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)$
As mentioned in the previous lines, self-duality of the critical model on  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$  ensures that  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(0)}[\omega_{e}]=\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p_{c}}[\omega_{e}]=\frac{1}{2}$  while  $\mathbf{p}_{e}(0)=p_{c}$ , which ensures that  $\mathbf{r}_{e}(0)=0$ . We now give the following estimate, which is the main improvement from the methods introduced in Section 3, which allows us to work with distributions  $\mathfrak{p}$  whose mean deviation is larger than square root of the deterministic one.
Lemma 4.2.
There exist a constant  $c=c(\delta,\rho,q)>0$  such that for any  $\sigma_{N}$  satisfying  ${\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)\log(N)^{-\frac{1}{2}}}$ , one has
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[\forall\,0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\forall\,e\in E_{N},\>|\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)|\leq\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\Bigg(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\Bigg)^{1/3}\right]\\
\geq 1-O_{\delta,\rho}\left(\exp\left[-c\left(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\sigma_{N}}\right)^{2}\right]\right).$
Proof.
For  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}$ , all of the bonds  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  are bounded away from  $0$  and  $1$ . Therefore, taking the expression of  $\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)$ , one may apply the triangular inequality to get for any  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}$ ,
$\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)\lesssim\Big|\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)-p_{c}\Big|+\Big|2\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]-1\Big|.$
Define the event
$G_{1}:=\Bigg\{\forall\,0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\>\Big|\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)-p_{c}\Big|\leq\varepsilon\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\Bigg(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\Bigg)^{1/3}\Bigg\}.$
The term  $|\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)-p_{c}|$  is the absolute value of a Brownian motion with a bounded drift started at  $0$ . Therefore, standard Brownian estimates ensure that for any  $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists  $c_{1}=c_{1}(\varepsilon)>0$  such that for any  $e\in\mathbb{T}_{N}$  one has
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\big[G_{1}\big]\\
\geq 1-O_{\delta,\rho,\varepsilon}\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-2c_{1}\cdot\Bigg(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\left(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\right)^{1/3}}{\sigma_{N}}\Bigg)^{\!2}\,\Bigg]\Bigg).$
Recalling that  $\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)\leq\textrm{W}(N)$  and  $\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\geq 1$ , one can take the union bound over edges  $e\in E_{N}$  and gets
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\big[G_{1}\big]\geq 1-O_{\delta,\rho,\varepsilon}\Bigg(N^{2}\exp\Bigg[-2c_{1}\cdot\left(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\sigma_{N}}\right)^{2}\Bigg]\Bigg)\geq 1-O_{\delta,\rho,\varepsilon}\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-c_{1}\cdot\left(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\sigma_{N}}\right)^{2}\Bigg]\Bigg),$
where the second inequality holds as  $\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\log(N)^{-1/2}$  with  $c>0$  small enough.
To complete the reasoning, let us estimate  $|2\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]-1|$ , by computing the stochastic derivative of the process  $t\mapsto\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]$ . We proceed again in several steps.
Step 0: Canonical decomposition of the semimartingale.
One can first decompose  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]:=M^{(e)}_{t}+A^{(e)}_{t}$  where  $M^{(e)}_{t}$  is a local martingale started at  $0$  and  $A^{(e)}_{t}$  is a bounded variation process started at  $\frac{1}{2}$ . Itô’s formula gives
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}M^{(e)}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{f\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{f}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{f}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\mathrm{d}B^{(f)}_{t},$
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}A^{(e)}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{f\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{f}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{f}(t))}\mathbf{r}_{f}(t)\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\mathrm{d}t.$
Step 1: Estimating the local martingale  $M^{(e)}_{t}$ .
For any  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}$ , one may use the stability of covariances and RSW to get that for  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}$ , one has
$\langle M^{(e)}\rangle_{t}\asymp t\sum_{r\leq N}r(\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2})^{2}=\left(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\right)t.$
Using once again large deviation estimates for local martingales, one gets that for any  $\varepsilon>0$ , there exist  $c_{1}>0$  such that for each edge  $e\in E_{N}$ ,
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[\forall\,0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\>|M^{(e)}_{t}|\leq\varepsilon\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\Bigg(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\Bigg)^{1/3}\right]\\
\geq 1-O_{\delta,\rho,\varepsilon}\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-c_{1}\cdot\Bigg(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\big(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\big)^{1/3}}{\big(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\big)^{1/2}\sigma_{N}}\Bigg)^{2}\Bigg]\Bigg)$
Defining the event
$G_{2}:=\Bigg\{\forall\,0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\forall\,e\in E_{N},\>|M^{(e)}_{t}|\leq\varepsilon\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\Bigg(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\Bigg)^{1/3}\Bigg\},$
recalling the definition of  $\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)$  and taking union bound over edges  $e\in E_{N}$  one gets
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\big[G_{2}\big]\geq 1-O_{\delta,\rho,\varepsilon}\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-c_{1}\cdot\left(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\sigma_{N}}\right)^{2}\Bigg]\Bigg).$
Step 2: Concluding the rate of growth of  $\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)$ .
One can now estimate the finite variation process  $A^{(e)}_{t}$  by integrating Itô’s formula. For any  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}$ , using that  $A^{\mathcal{R}}_{0}=\frac{1}{2}$ , one has
$\displaystyle\left|A^{(e)}_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\right|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}\sup_{f\in E_{N}}|\mathbf{r}_{f}(t)|\right)\left(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2}\right)t$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b})}\sup_{f\in E_{N}}|\mathbf{r}_{f}(t)|\right)\Xi(N)^{-1}\sigma_{N}^{2},$
where the first inequality uses (3.3), the comparability of the edge covariances with their critical counterparts (as  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}$ ) and their sum over  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$  for the critical measure recalled in Remark 2.10. Going back to the bound on  $\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)$ , one gets
$\displaystyle\sup_{t,e}|\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sup_{t,e}|\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)-p_{c}|+\sup_{t,e}\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]-\frac{1}{2}\right|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sup_{t,e}|\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)-p_{c}|+\sup_{t,e}|M^{(e)}_{t}|+\sup_{t,e}\left|A^{(e)}_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\right|$
where the above supremum  $\sup_{t,e}$  is taken over times  $0\leq t\leq(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho))$  and edges  $e\in E_{N}$ . On the event  $G_{1}\cap G_{2}$  one has
$\sup_{t,e}|\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)|\lesssim\varepsilon\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\Big(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\Big)^{1/3}+\Xi(N)^{-1}\sigma_{N}^{2}\Big(\sup_{t,e}|\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)|\Big).$
One can then apply Lemma 2.12 which states that
$\Xi(N)^{-1}\sigma_{N}^{2}\lesssim\Xi(N)^{-1}\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{2/3}}{\log(N)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\lesssim\frac{1}{\log(N)^{\frac{1}{2}}}.$
For  $N$  large enough, one can conclude that
$\sup_{t,e}|\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)|\leq O\Big(\varepsilon\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\Big(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\Big)^{1/3}\Big)+\frac{1}{2}\sup_{t,e}|\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)|.$
Choosing  $\varepsilon>0$  small enough such that  $1/(2\varepsilon)$  is larger than the implicit constant in the  $O$ , one gets
$\sup_{t,e}|\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)|\leq\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\Big(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\Big)^{1/3}.$
The estimates on the respective probabilities of  $G_{1}$  and  $G_{2}$  allow to conclude the proof.
∎
4.1.3 Completing the proof of Proposition 4.1
We are in position to prove Proposition 4.1 in the spirit of the proofs made in Section 3.1, sorting out natural counterparts to Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4. We will once again show that with high  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$ -probability, the breaking time  $T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$  is large enough, finding some  $\delta,\rho$  such that
$\mathbf{P}\Big[T_{b}(\delta,\rho)<\sigma_{N}^{2}\Big]\lesssim\exp\Bigg[-c\left(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\sigma_{N}}\right)^{2}\Bigg].$
(4.3)
This reads on the following lemmas.
Lemma 4.3.
Assume that  $\delta$  is chosen small enough, only depending on  $1<q\leq 4$ . Then for any  $\rho>0$ , there are some positive constants  $c=c(\delta,\rho,q)$  and  $O_{\delta,\rho}(\cdot)$  such that, provided  $\sigma_{N}^{2}\leq c\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\log(N)^{-1}$ , one has
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall\,0\leq s\leq\Big(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)\Big),\,\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta,\rho}\left(\exp\Bigg[-c\cdot\left(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\sigma_{N}}\right)^{2}\Bigg]\right).$
The same result holds when replacing  $\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)$  by the stability events  $\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(2\delta,N)$  for  $\#\in\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\textrm{rg}},3^{\textrm{lf}}\}$ .
Lemma 4.4.
Assume that  $\delta$  is chosen small enough, only depending on  $1<q\leq 4$ .
Then there exists a constant  $\rho=\rho(\delta)>0$  small enough and some positive constants  $c=c(\delta,\rho(\delta),q)>0$  and  $O_{\delta,\rho}(\cdot)$  such that provided  $\sigma_{N}^{2}\leq c\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\log(N)^{-1}$ ,
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall\,0\leq s\leq\Big(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)\Big),\,\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(2\rho,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta,\rho}\left(\exp\Bigg[-c\cdot\left(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\sigma_{N}}\right)^{2}\Bigg]\right).$
We now pass to the proof of the those two lemmas, skipping the details regarding the potential degeneracies between  $\delta$  and  $\rho(\delta)$ , as they can be tracked exactly as in the proof of Lemma 3.4. In particular, to lighten the reading, we also remove the  $\delta,\rho$  dependencies in the constants  $\lesssim$  and  $\asymp$ .
