We keep exactly the structure of the previous proofs, and mostly focus on evaluating how the introduction of the drift lowers the order of magnitude of the finite variation process.
Proof of Lemma 4.3.
Let us start by proving the announced statement for  $\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$  when  $\bullet\in\{h,v\}$ . A similar reasoning allows to conclude once again for arm events, in the spirit of the arguments presented at the end of Lemma 3.3.
Step 0: Canonical decomposition of the semimartingale.
Fix again a  $2$  by  $1$  rectangle  $\mathcal{R}\in\mathbb{T}_{N}$  of width smaller than  $N/8$  and consider the event  $\mathcal{S}=\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$ . We may apply Itô’s formula to the Brownian motions with drifts  $\big((B^{(e)}_{t}-\mu(q)t)_{t\geq 0}\big)_{e\in E_{N}}$  to get
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{S}]$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}\bigg\rvert_{\underline{p}=\mathfrak{p}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p}}[\mathcal{S}]\right)\mathrm{d}B^{(e)}_{t}-\mu(q)\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}\bigg\rvert_{\underline{p}=\mathfrak{p}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p}}[\mathcal{S}]\right)\mathrm{d}t$
$\displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{2}\Bigg(\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\left(\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{e}^{2}}\bigg\rvert_{\underline{p}=\mathfrak{p}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p}}[\mathcal{S}]\right)\Bigg)\mathrm{d}t,$
$\displaystyle=\mathrm{d}M_{t}^{\mathcal{R}}+\mathrm{d}A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t},$
where  $M^{\mathcal{R}}$  is a local martingale started at  $0$  and  $A^{\mathcal{R}}$  is a finite variation process. Using Proposition 2.13, the associated explicit expressions read as
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}B^{(e)}_{t}$
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}t.$
We evaluate again the order of magnitude of  $M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$  and  $A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$  for times  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}$  using the results of Section 2.5.
Step 1: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$ .
In this first step, we assume that the event  $G_{1}\cap G_{2}$  of Lemma 4.2 holds, which happens with high probability. In that setup, for any  $e\in E_{N}$  and any  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}$  one has  $|\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)|\lesssim\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\left(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\right)^{1/3}$ . This ensures that for  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}$  one has
$\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\lesssim\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\Big(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\Big)^{1/3}\sum_{e\in E}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\lesssim\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{-2/3},$
where we used Lemma 2.14 to apply (2.22) and the exact expression of  $\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)$ . Integrating the previous equation, still intersecting with the event  $G_{1}\cap G_{2}$  of Lemma 4.2, one has for  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}$  and  $\sigma_{N}\lesssim\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\log(N)^{-1/2}$  that
$|A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}-A^{\mathcal{R}}_{0}|\lesssim\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{-2/3}\cdot t\lesssim\log(N)^{-1}.$
Step 2: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$ .
The estimates here are exactly the same as in the proof of Lemma 3.3, and give that for all  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}$ ,
$\frac{d}{\mathrm{d}t}\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}\lesssim\Xi(N)^{-1}.$
Applying Lemma 2.12 to get  $\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)$  to appear and integrating gives that
$\forall\,0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\quad\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}\lesssim\left(\frac{\sigma_{N}}{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}\right)^{2}.$
Once the bounds of Step  $1$  and  $2$  on the two components of  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]$ , one can apply verbatim the same large deviation principle, asserting that if  $T_{b}$  is too small, then at least one of the local martingales associated to a crossing deviated from its initial value too fast compared to what its bracket typically allows, which happens with very small probability. Finally, as in the proof of Lemma 3.3, the previous proof adapts exactly to the case of stability of arm events.
∎
We now move to the proof of Lemma 4.4, inspired by the one of Lemma 3.4.
Proof of Lemma 4.4.
Once again, one should in principle specify all the  $\delta,\rho$  dependencies in the constants of the proof, but one can replicate the reasoning at the end of the proof of Lemma 3.4 to show that one can always choose  $\rho=\rho(\delta)>0$  small enough provided  $\delta>0$  and still run all the arguments.
Step 0: Canonical decomposition of the semimartingale.
Fix two edges  $e,f\in E$  at distance  $R$  from each other. Applying Itô’s formula gives  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})=M^{e,f}_{t}+A^{e,f}_{t}$  where  $M^{e,f}$  is a local martingale started at  $0$  and  $A^{e,f}$  is an adapted process with bounded variation, whose stochastic derivatives are given by
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}M^{e,f}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{g}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{g}(t))}\kappa^{\mathfrak{p}(t)}_{3}(e,f,g)\mathrm{d}B^{(g)}_{t},$
$\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}A^{e,f}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{g}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{g}(t))}\mathbf{r}_{g}(t)\kappa^{\mathfrak{p}(t)}_{3}(e,f,g)$
$\displaystyle\quad-\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{g}(t)^{2}(1-\mathbf{p}_{g}(t))^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g}).$
Step 1: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $A^{e,f}_{t}$ .
Once again we assume that the high probability event  $G_{1}\cap G_{2}$  of Lemma 4.2 holds, allowing us to assume that for any  $g\in E_{N}$  one has  $|\mathbf{r}_{g}(t)|\lesssim\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\left(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\right)^{1/3}$ . We can then run the computations as in the proof of Lemma 3.4, while adding the improved bound on the  $\mathbf{r}_{g}(t)$ . One gets for  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}$ ,
$\displaystyle\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}A^{e,f}_{t}\right|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\Big(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\Big)^{1/3}\Bigg(\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\kappa^{\mathfrak{p}(t)}_{3}(e,f,g)\Bigg)$
$\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pt+\sum_{g\in E}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g})$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}\Big(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\Big)^{1/3}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}+\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{-2/3}.$
Passing to the last line one uses the definition of  $\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)$  and Lemma 2.12. Integrating the previous bound on the event  $G_{1}\cap G_{2}$  of Lemma 4.2 ensures that provided  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}$ , one has
$|A^{e,f}_{t}-A^{e,f}_{0}|\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\log(N)^{-1}.$
Step 2: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $M^{e,f}_{t}$ .
One can now compute the bracket of the local martingale  $M^{e,f}$ , which is given by
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\langle M^{e,f}\rangle_{t}=\sum_{g\in E}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{g}(t)^{2}(1-\mathbf{p}_{g}(t))^{2}}\kappa^{\mathfrak{p}(t)}_{3}(e,f,g)^{2}.$
Once again, we can use (2.30) to get
$\forall\,0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\quad\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\langle M^{e,f}\rangle_{t}\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{4}\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1}.$
Using Lemma 2.12 to make  $\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)$  appear, and integrating in  $t$  gives
$\forall\,0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\quad\langle M^{e,f}\rangle_{t}\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{4}\left(\frac{\sigma_{N}}{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}\right)^{2}$
Once the bounds of Step  $1$  and  $2$  on the two components of  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$ , one can apply again the same large deviation principle, asserting that if  $T_{b}$  is too small, again some local martingale deviated too fast compared to what its bracket allows, which concludes the proof.
∎
4.2 General random variables satisfying  $(\star)^{\textmd{B}}_{N}$
Once the special case of Gaussian variables with natural centring around  $p_{c}(q)$  is settled, one can prove Theorem 1.6 in the general case, in the spirit of proof made in Section 3.2. We start by fixing some random environment  $\mathfrak{p}$  over  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$  that satisfies  $(\star)^{\text{B}}_{N}$ , where the standard deviations also satisfy  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}\leq c\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\log(N)^{-2}$  for some small enough constant  $c>0$ . The strategy of the proof can be summarised as follows. We still wish to construct a continuous family of random environment  $\mathfrak{p}(t)$ , starting from the critical one and traveling towards  $\mathfrak{p}$ . We will this time generalise (3.12), setting
$\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)=p_{c}+B^{(e)}_{t\wedge T^{(e)}}-\mu^{(e)}\cdot(t\wedge T^{(e)}),$
where  $\big((B^{(e)}_{t})_{t\geq 0}\big)_{e\in E_{N}}$  are i.i.d standard brownian motions, the variables  $(T^{(e)})_{e\in E_{N}}$  are some almost-surely finite stopping times and the deterministic constants  $\mu^{(e)}$  will be cleverly chosen (via  $\mathfrak{p}$ ) to that  $\mathbf{p}_{e}(\infty)=\mathbf{p}_{e}$ . In this formalism, Section 4.1 can be viewed as a special case where the spotting times  $(T^{(e)})_{e\in E_{N}}$  are all equal to some deterministic  $T>0$ . Before diving into the construction of the variables  $(T^{(e)})_{e\in E_{N}}$ , le us run some preliminary computations.
We claim that, for each edge  $e\in E_{N}$ , the exist  $\mu^{(e)}>0$  such that
$\mathbb{E}[e^{2\mu^{(e)}\cdot(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q))}]=1.$
Let us first prove the existence of  $\mu^{(e)}$  and derive its expansion.
Fix  $e\in E_{N}$  and consider the function  $\mu\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\mapsto\mathbb{E}[e^{2\mu\cdot(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q))}]$ . The function is equal to  $1$  for  $\mu=0$ , has a derivative  $2\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q)]<0$  at  $0$ , is convex, and tends to  $+\infty$  as  $\mu\to+\infty$ . Therefore, there exist a unique  $\mu^{(e)}>0$  such that  $\mathbb{E}[e^{2\mu^{(e)}\cdot(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q))}]=1$ . One can use the exponential tail bonds on  $|\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q)|$ , which allows us to expand for  $\mu\lesssim 1$ ,
$\mathbb{E}[e^{2\mu(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q))}]=1+2\mu\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q)]+2\mu^{2}\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q))^{2}]+O(\mu^{3}\sigma_{e}^{3})$
Notice that  $2\mu\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q)]\asymp-\mu\sigma_{e}^{2}$  while  $2\mu^{2}\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q))^{2}]\asymp\mu^{2}\sigma_{e}^{2}$ . Since  $\sigma_{e}\to 0$  uniformly in edges  $e\in\mathbb{T}_{N}$  as  $N\to\infty$ , the asymptotics give that if  $\mu$  is large enough (but still of constant order),then  $\mathbb{E}[e^{2\mu\cdot(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q))}]>1$ , and hence  $\mu^{(e)}\lesssim 1$ . Plugging the definition of  $\mu^{(e)}$  in the above expansion one gets
$1=\mathbb{E}[e^{2\mu^{(e)}\cdot(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q))}]=1+2\mu^{(e)}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q)]+2(\mu^{(e)})^{2}\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q))^{2}]+O((\mu^{(e)})^{3}\sigma_{e}^{3})$
which implies that
$-\mu^{(e)}\mu(q)\sigma_{e}^{2}+(\mu^{(e)})^{2}\sigma_{e}^{2}=O((\mu^{(e)})^{3}\sigma_{e}^{3})$
and finally (dividing by  $\mu^{(e)}\lesssim 1$ ) ensures that
$\mu^{(e)}=\mu(q)+O(\sigma_{e}).$
(4.4)
Define the time parametrised random environment
$\mathbf{p}_{e}(t):=p_{c}(q)+B_{t\wedge T^{(e)}}^{(e)}-\mu^{(e)}\cdot(t\wedge T^{(e)}),$
where the stopping time  $T^{(e)}$  will be constructed below to satisfy  $\mathbf{p}_{e}=\mathbf{p}_{e}(\infty)$ . One can now prove Theorem 1.6 exactly as we did for Proposition 4.1, modulo the ability to derive some extra estimates on the tails of the collection  $(T^{(e)})_{e\in E_{N}}$ . We construct explicitly the family  $(T^{(e)})_{e\in E_{N}}$ , which allows us to control their tails via the control of the tails of the variables  $\mathfrak{p}$ , with the minor downside that our stopping times may now be infinite with positive probability. The result we obtain is the following.
Lemma 4.5.
Let  $X$  be some real valued random variable such that  $|X|\leq 1$  and  $\mu$  such that  $\mathbb{E}[e^{2\mu X}]=1$ . We also assume that  $X$  has a tail
$\forall t>0,\quad\mathbb{P}[X>t]\lesssim\exp\Big[-c\cdot(t/\sigma)^{\gamma}\Big],$
for some positive constants  $\sigma\leq 1$  and  $\gamma$ . Let  $(B_{t})_{t\geq 0}$  be a standard Brownian motion for the filtration  $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ . Then there exists a stopping time  $T$  for  $(B_{t})_{t\geq 0}$  such that:
•
One may couple the pair  $\big((B_{t})_{t\geq 0},T\big)$  and  $X$  such that, on the event  $\{T<\infty\}$ , one has
$B_{T}-\mu T\overset{(d)}{=}X$ .
•
The exists positive constants  $\lesssim,\tilde{c}$ , only depending on  $c,\gamma$  and the fact that  $\mu$  is uniformly bounded away from  $0$  and  $\pm\infty$ , such that for all  $t>0$
$\mathbb{P}\Big[T>t\Big]\lesssim\exp\Big[-\tilde{c}\cdot\sigma^{-\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+1}}\Big]+\exp\Big[-\tilde{c}\Big(\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}}\Big)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\Big].$
In the setup of variables satisfying  $(\star)_{N}^{\text{B}}$  and for  $X^{(e)}$  a random variable of distribution  $\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}$ , one can take  $\gamma=1$ , while the variables  $\mu^{(e)}$  remain bounded away from  $0$  and  $\pm\infty$  (as a consequence of the preliminary computations). Denoting by  $T^{(e)}$  the stopping time constructed for the variable  $X^{(e)}$  and the Brownian motion  $(B^{(e)}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ , one has
$\forall t>0,\quad\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[T^{(e)}>t\Bigg]\lesssim\exp\left[-c^{\prime}\cdot\left(\frac{t}{\sigma_{e}^{2}}\right)^{1/3}\right]+\exp\Bigg[-c^{\prime}\sigma_{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\Bigg].$
In general, using Lemma 3.7 to bound  $\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha_{e}T^{(e)}$  is very inefficient, as one single coefficient  $\alpha_{e}$  could be of the order of magnitude of  $\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\alpha_{e}$ . Instead, we use the most naive union bound on the supremum of the  $(T^{(e)})_{e\in E_{N}}$ . This reads as
$\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\sup_{e\in E_{N}}T^{(e)}>\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/2}\Bigg]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim N^{2}\left(\exp\left[-c^{\prime}\cdot\left(\frac{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}}\right)^{1/3}\right]+\exp\Bigg[-c^{\prime}\cdot\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-1/2}\Bigg]\right)$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}c^{\prime}\cdot\left(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\right]+\exp\Bigg(-\frac{1}{2}c^{\prime}\cdot\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-1/2}\Bigg)$
where the passage to the last line uses that  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}\leq c\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\log(N)^{-2}$ . Conditioning on the event
$\Bigg\{\sup_{e\in E_{N}}T^{(e)}\leq\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/2}\Bigg\},$
one can reproduce almost verbatim the proof of Proposition 4.1 using  $\left(\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/2}\right)^{1/2}$  to replace  $\sigma_{N}$ . The only notable difference in the computation is the appearance of some additional term in the Itô derivatives, which we detail now. For an event  $\mathcal{S}$ , the presence of the drift gives that
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{S}]$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}B^{(e)}_{t}$
$\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}t$
$\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{e\in E_{N}}(\mu^{(e)}-\mu(q))\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}t$
Recalling that (4.4), one can bound  $|\mu^{(e)}-\mu(q)|=O(\sigma_{e})\lesssim\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}$ , and this upper bound is smaller than the one obtained for  $\mathbf{r}_{e}(t)$  in Section 4.1.2, so one can apply the same proof. Therefore, there exists  $c>0$  small enough such that such that provided  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}$  is chosen to satisfy
$\big(\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/2}\big)^{1/2}\leq c\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\log(N)^{-1/2}$ , or equivalently  ${\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}\leq c^{4}\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\log(N)^{-2}}$ ,
$\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Bigg]$
$\displaystyle>1-O\left(\exp\left[-c\cdot\left(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\left(\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/2}\right)^{1/2}}\right)^{\!2}\,\right]\right)$
$\displaystyle\geq 1-O\left(\exp\left[-c\cdot\left(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{\!1/2}\right]\right).$
Combining all observations made above allows us to conclude the proof of Theorem 1.6.
4.3 Optimality of the random bond near-critical window
In the previous section, we showed that strengthening the condition  $(\star)^{\text{A}}_{N}$  to  $(\star)^{\text{B}}_{N}$  allows us to use a random a random environment where the bonds have a much larger standard deviation. We now explain that a critical window in a random environment of order  $\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}$  is “essentially optimal”, in the sense that finding a condition on the (independent) random bond environment  $\mathfrak{p}$  to enlarge the critical window would require some much more refined understanding than simply the up to constant behaviour of crossing estimates, mixing rates and arm exponents.
Let us start by discussion how the  $O(\sigma_{e}^{3})$  correction term in condition  $(\star)^{\text{B}}_{N}$  naturally appears. In the special case  $q=1$ , the results of
Section 5 show that the natural condition on the independent random bond parameters is that  $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{p}_{e}]=\frac{1}{2}$ , which allows us to preserve the critical phase of the model (at large scale) even with random variables whose standard variation does not decay to  $0$  as  $N\to\infty$ . When remaining in the near-critical random setup, one may expect that this “criticality condition” generalises to  $q>1$ , in the sense that there should exist  $f=f_{q}$  some smooth function depending on  $q$  such that the natural condition on the parameters  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  to preserve criticality at large scales is given by  $\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{p}_{e})]=0$ . While  $f_{1}$  is easy to guess as it corresponds to asking that the annealed model is critical Bernoulli percolation, this requires some more evolved reasoning when  $q>1$ . For  $q>1$ , the critical point  $p_{c}(q)$  is determined by the fact that it is the self-dual point of the model. In this spirit, the condition we require on  $f_{q}$  is that  $\mathbb{E}[f_{q}(\mathbf{p})]=0$  for any random variable  $\mathbf{p}$  which is self-dual for the FK percolation model. By self-dual, we mean that  $\mathbf{p}$  and  $\mathbf{p}^{*}$  have the same law, where
$\mathbf{p}^{*}:=\frac{q(1-\mathbf{p})}{\mathbf{p}+q(1-\mathbf{p})}$
is the dual parameter of  $\mathbf{p}$ . Taking  $\mathbf{p}:=\frac{1}{2}\delta_{p}+\frac{1}{2}\delta_{p^{*}}$  for  $p\in[0,1]$ , this implies that  $f_{q}$  must satisfy
$\forall p\in[0,1],\quad f_{q}(p^{*})=-f_{q}(p).$
(4.5)
In the near-critical setup  $\varepsilon\to 0$ , one can expand near the critical point  $p_{c}=p_{c}(q)$  the relation  $f_{q}((p_{c}+\varepsilon)^{*})=-f_{q}(p_{c}+\varepsilon)$ , which implies that
$f_{q}\left(p_{c}-\varepsilon-\frac{q-1}{\sqrt{q}}\varepsilon^{2}-\frac{(q-1)^{2}}{q}\varepsilon^{3}-\ldots\right)=-f_{q}(p_{c})-\varepsilon f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c})-\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}f_{q}^{\prime\prime}(p_{c})-\frac{\varepsilon^{3}}{6}f^{(3)}_{q}(p_{c})+\ldots,$
which reads as
$2f_{q}(p_{c})+0\cdot\varepsilon+\left(f_{q}^{\prime\prime}(p_{c})-\frac{q-1}{\sqrt{q}}f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c})\right)\varepsilon^{2}+\left(\frac{q-1}{\sqrt{q}}f_{q}^{\prime\prime}(p_{c})-\frac{(q-1)^{2}}{q}f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c})\right)\varepsilon^{3}+\ldots=0$
(4.6)
The above equation shows that if one wants to cancel all the coefficients in the expansion, although there are infinitely many conditions on the derivatives of  $f_{q}$  at  $p_{c}$ , these conditions are not sufficient to uniquely determine  $f_{q}$ . For every  $n\geq 1$ , the condition (4.6) imposes an equation linking the first  $2n$  derivatives at  $p_{c}$ , but with infinitely many degrees of freedom for  $f_{q}$ . Indeed, one can freely choose the odd degree derivatives of  $f_{q}$  at  $p_{c}$ , which is enough to fix the derivatives of even degree. This can be seen by interpreting (4.5) as asking, up to conjugation by some smooth map, that  $f_{q}$  is an odd function, whose odd derivatives at zero (corresponding to  $p_{c}$  under the conjugation) can be chosen arbitrarily, and even derivatives at zero are forced to cancel.
Let us now specify those conditions for the first derivatives of  $f_{q}$ . This clearly imposes that  $f_{q}(p_{c})=0$ . One can always replace  $f_{q}$  by a constant multiple and still satisfy (4.5), which allws us to arbitrarily fix the value of  $f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c})$ . Then, (4.6) imposes that  $f_{q}^{\prime\prime}(p_{c})=\frac{q-1}{\sqrt{q}}f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c})$ . Assuming that  $f_{q}$  is at least three times differentiable at  $p_{c}$ , plugging in some variable  $\mathbf{p}$  well concentrated around  $p_{c}$  in the equation  $\mathbb{E}[f_{q}(\mathbf{p})]=0$ , one gets
$f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c})\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{p}-p_{c}]+\frac{f_{q}^{\prime\prime}(p_{c})}{2}\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{p}-p_{c})^{2}]+O(\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{p}-p_{c})^{2}]^{3/2})=0$
The link between  $f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c})$  and  $f_{q}^{\prime\prime}(p_{c})$  precisely gives item  $2\textrm{B})$  in Definition 1.3.
Now although we do not claim that there does not exist some function  $f_{q}$  allowing us to have environments which stay critical in a window of size larger than  $\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}$ , we explain why a generic choice of a function  $f_{q}$  satisfying (4.5) cannot allow us to go further than  $\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}$ . Pick a generic  $f_{q}$  satisfying (4.5) and an environment  $\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in e_{N}}$  of i.i.d.​ bond parameters such that  $\mathbb{E}[f_{q}(\mathbf{p}_{e})]=0$ , and assume by contradiction that the environment can be chosen such that  $\sigma_{e}\gg\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}$ . Now consider the deterministic modification of the environment  $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}=\mathbf{p}_{e}+\sigma_{e}^{3}$ . Since  $\mathbb{E}[f_{q}(\mathbf{p}_{e})]=0$ , one clearly has  $\mathbb{E}[f_{q}(\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e})]=O(\sigma_{e}^{3})$ . It is not hard to see that it is possible to construct a function  $\widetilde{f}_{q}$ , satisfying (4.5) as  $\varepsilon\to 0$  in the following way: under the conjugation map where (4.5) becomes the condition that  $f_{q}$  is odd, one may pick  $\widetilde{f}_{q}(x)=f_{q}(x)-\alpha x^{3}$  for some well chosen  $\alpha$ . In this construction,  $\widetilde{f}_{q}$  obviously depends on the law of the  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  (and so on  $N$  as well), but one may check that  $\alpha$  is bounded uniformly in  $\sigma_{e}$ , so that even as  $N\to\infty$  and  $\sigma_{e}\to 0$ , one may still consider  $\widetilde{f}_{q}$  to be a generic function satisfying (4.5). Now since  $\widetilde{f}_{q}$  is a generic function satisfying (4.5), under our assumption, the environment  $\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}=(\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}$  should still have some  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  property on the torus  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$ . However, between the environments  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  and  $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}$ , the coupling constant differ deterministically by a positive constant  $\sigma_{e}^{3}\gg\textrm{W}(N)$ . In particular, assuming  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  remains in the critical phase (with high  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$ -probability), this deterministic modification, way above the critical window, imposes that the model with environment  $\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}$  should be super-critical (with high  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$ -probability), by simply repeating all the arguments in the proof Theorem 2.3 starting from  $\mathfrak{p}$  instead of  $p_{c}$ , and keeping track of the reverse inequalities (see also [25, Section 5]). This is a contradiction, and so a generic choice of  $f_{q}$  could not lead to critical windows larger than  $\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}$  for the random environment.
4.4 Non-independent bonds and extension of the critical window
In this section, we explore the less restrictive setup of bond parameters at each edge that may not be independent. On  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$ , we work in a setup where the bonds can be seen as the sum of an i.i.d process at each edge and some (much smaller) correction drift involving the entire random environment in  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$ . Consider stochastic processes of the form  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{S}]$ , similar to the one treated in Sections 3.1 and 4.1. One of the key observation when computing  $\mathrm{d}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{S}]$  is that, with high  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$  probability, its dominant term is its finite variation part. Our specific choice of the drift is made here to cancel exactly that drift, making of the processes of the form  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathscr{C}(S)]$  pure local martingale, whose stochastic derivatives (estimated via their brackets) are expected to be much smaller, allowing to run some controlled at each scale deformation for a much longer amount of time. In this section, recall the quantity  $\Xi(N)=(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2})^{-1}$ . Let us note that the inequality  $\Xi(N)\gtrsim\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{2/3}$  is essentially sharp (up to subpolynomial factors) when  $\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\gtrsim R^{-1/2+o(1)}$ , but assuming that  $\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\lesssim R^{-1/2-c}$  for some  $c>0$  (which should be the case for  $q<4$ ), the inequality should hold with an additional polynomial correction  $\Xi(N)\gtrsim N^{c^{\prime}}\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{2/3}$ , and so the window reached in the following proposition is much larger than that of the previous section. Once again, we start by presenting a simplified version of the Theorem in the case where the random environment  $\mathfrak{p}$  is Gaussian.
Proposition 4.6.
Fix  $1<q\leq 4$  and let  $\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E}$  a random environment satisfying (4.1). There exist some positive constants  $\delta,O,c_{1,2}$  such that if  $\sigma_{N}\leq c_{1}\cdot\Xi(N)^{1/2}\log(N)^{-1/2}$ , one can construct some random environment  $\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}=(\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}$  such that
•
Under  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$ , for each  $e\in E_{N}$ , the difference  $|\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}-\mathbf{p}_{e}|$  is of order  $\Xi(N)^{-1/2}\sigma_{N}^{3}$ , in the sense that
$\forall\alpha>0,\quad\mathbf{P}_{N}\Big[|\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}-\mathbf{p}_{e}|>\alpha\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1/2}\sigma_{N}^{3}\Big]\lesssim\exp(-c\alpha^{2}).$
•
One has
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Big[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Big]>1-O\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-c_{2}\cdot\left(\frac{\Xi(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{2}\Bigg]\Bigg).$
Let us comment on the implications of this statement. Informally speaking, Theorem 1.7 states that, one can correct at each edge the i.i.d Gaussian, whose typical order of magnitude is  $\sigma_{N}$ , by some random factor, depending on entire environment  $\mathfrak{p}$ , whose typical order of magnitude is  $\Xi(N)^{-1/2}\cdot\sigma_{N}^{3}\ll\sigma_{N}$ , while enlarging the critical window in random environment. Using the CLE predictions (asserting that  $\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\lesssim R^{-\frac{1}{2}-c}$  for  $q<4$ ), one expects this enlargement to be at least of polynomial order  $1<q<4$ . For  $1<q\leq 2$ , one expects the critical window in the random environment to be, with high probability, of logarithmic order. Indeed, it is conjectured that  $\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\lesssim R^{-1-c}$  for  $q<2$  ensuring that  $\Xi(N)\asymp 1$ . For the limiting case  $q=2$ , it is known that  $\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\asymp R^{-1}$ , so that  $\Xi(N)\asymp\log(N)^{-1}$ .
Proof of Proposition 4.6.
We will once again embed  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  as a Brownian motion with some drift, given by
$\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)=p_{c}+B^{(e)}_{t}-\mu(q)t$
and couple the Brownian motions with  $\mathfrak{p}$  such that for each  $e\in E_{N}$  one has  $\mathbf{p}_{e}(\sigma_{N}^{2})=\mathbf{p}_{e}$ . From now on, define, on the same probability space, the process  $\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)=(\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t))_{e\in E_{N}}$  via
$\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)=\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)+\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)$
where  $t\mapsto(\varepsilon^{(e)}(t))_{e\in E_{N}}$  is an (adapted) continuously differentiable process such that for any  $e\in E_{N}$ , one has  $\varepsilon^{(e)}(0)=0$  and  $(\varepsilon^{(e)}(t))_{e\in E_{N}}$  satisfies the SDE
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)=\mu(q)\cdot t-\frac{1}{1-\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)}\left(1-\frac{1}{\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]\right).$
(4.7)
The stochastic differential system satisfied by  $(\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)_{t\geq 0})_{e\in E_{N}}$  involves the entire environment via  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]$ , making the bonds parameters in  $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}=\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(\sigma_{N}^{2})$  not independent from each other. In this setup, we once again use the notation  $T_{b}=T_{b}(\delta,\rho)$  from the previous sections.
For an event  $\mathcal{S}$ , one can write the random process  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\mathcal{S}]=M^{\mathcal{S}}_{t}+A^{\mathcal{S}}_{t}$  where  $M^{\mathcal{S}}$  is a local martingale started at  $0$  and  $A^{\mathcal{S}}$  is an adapted process with bounded variation. The (a priori unnatural) choice of  $(\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)_{t\geq 0})_{e\in E_{N}}$  is made to leave  $A^{\mathcal{S}}_{t}$  constant, meaning that
$\displaystyle\frac{d}{\mathrm{d}t}A^{\mathcal{S}}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)(1-\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t))^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]\right)\mathrm{Cov}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e})$
$\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)(1-\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t))}\left(-\mu^{(e)}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)\right)\mathrm{Cov}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e})$
$\displaystyle=0.$
Therefore, all the  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\mathcal{S}]=M^{\mathcal{S}}_{t}+A^{\mathcal{S}}_{t}$  are pure local martingales, whose bracket is given by
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\langle\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\mathcal{S}]\rangle_{t}=\sum_{e\in E}\frac{1}{\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)^{2}(1-\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t))^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e})^{2}.$
To conclude, it is enough to prove that one can chose positive constants  $\delta,\rho$  such that the event  $T_{b}>\sigma_{N}^{2}$  happens with high  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$  probability. The proofs are very close to those of Propositions 3.1 and 4.1, allowing us to only make a sketch.
Step 1: Estimating the quadratic variation of  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]$  and  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\mathcal{A}^{(e)}_{\#}(R)]$ .
For each  $2$  by  $1$  rectangle  $\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}$  and any  $\bullet\in\{h,v\}$ , the process  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]$  is a local martingale, whose quadratic variation is given by
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\langle\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(\cdot)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\rangle_{t}=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)^{2}(1-\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t))^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}$
For  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}$ , we may use Lemma 2.8 and then integrate in time to deduce that
$\langle\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(\cdot)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\rangle_{t}\lesssim\Xi(N)^{-1}\cdot t.$
Similarly, using Remark 2.10, one gets that for any  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}$ , any  $e\in E_{N}$ ,  $R\leq N/4$  and any  $\#\in\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\textrm{lf}},3^{\textrm{rg}}\}$  one has
$\langle\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(\cdot)}[\mathcal{A}^{(e)}_{\#}(R)]\rangle_{t}\lesssim\pi_{\#,p_{c}}(R)^{2}\Xi(N)^{-1}\cdot t.$
Step 2: Estimates for  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$ .
Fix two edges  $e,f\in E_{N}$  at distance  $R$  from each other. The process  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$  is not a local martingale, so we decompose it into  $M^{e,f}_{t}+A^{e,f}_{t}$  where  $M^{e,f}_{t}$  is a local martingale started at  $0$  and  $A^{e,f}_{t}$  is an adapted process with bounded variation.
Step 2.1: Estimating the bounded variation term  $A^{e,f}_{t}$ .
Using the Itô’s formula gives the derivative of  $A^{e,f}_{t}$ . Note that most terms cancel out, and the only term left is
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}A^{e,f}_{t}=-\sum_{g\in E}\frac{1}{\widetilde{\mathbf{p}_{g}}(t)^{2}(1-\widetilde{\mathbf{p}_{g}}(t))^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g}).$
For  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}$ , we may estimate this term by (2.31) and integrating in  $t$ , which gives
$|A^{e,f}_{t}-A^{e,f}_{0}|\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\frac{t}{\Xi(N)}.$
Step 2.2: Estimating the local martingale term  $M^{e,f}_{t}$ .
Itô’s formula gives that
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\langle M^{e,f}\rangle_{t}=\sum_{g\in E}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{g}(t)^{2}(1-\mathbf{p}_{g}(t))^{2}}\kappa^{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}_{3}(e,f,g)^{2}.$
Applying (2.30) and integrating up to  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}$  gives that
$\langle M^{e,f}\rangle_{t}\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{4}\frac{t}{\Xi(N)}.$
Step 3: Concluding via Gronwall’s lemma.
The above estimates allow to concludes as in Propositions 3.1 and 4.1. Still, one should check that the bond parameters  $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}$  indeed remain close to  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$ , by bounding the terms  $\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)$ . Assume now that  $T_{b}>\sigma_{N}^{2}$ . This can be done by noticing that as long as  $\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)$  remains away from  $0$  and  $1$ , one has for  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}$
$\displaystyle\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)\right|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim|\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)-p_{c}|+\left|\phi_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]-\frac{1}{2}\right|$
$\displaystyle\lesssim|B^{(e)}_{t}|+t+|\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)|+\left|\phi_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]-\frac{1}{2}\right|$
One can bound the linear term  $t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}$ , while, with probability at least  $\exp(-c\alpha^{2})$ , one can bound  $\sup_{t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}}|B_{t}^{(e)}|\leq\alpha\cdot\sigma_{N}$  for all edges  $e\in E_{N}$ . Repeating Step  $1$  of the present proof ensures that with probability at least  $1-\exp(-c\alpha^{2})$ , we can bound
$\sup_{t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}}\left|\phi_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]-\frac{1}{2}\right|$  by  $\alpha\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1/2}\sigma_{N}$ . Therefore, with probability at least  $1-\exp(-c\alpha^{2})$ , one has for any  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}$ ,
$\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)\right|\lesssim|\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)|+\alpha\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1/2}\sigma_{N}.$
Using Gronwall’s lemma up to time  $t=\sigma_{N}^{2}\ll 1$  ensures that, with probability at least  $1-\exp(-c\alpha^{2})$ , for any  $0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}$ ,
$|\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}-\mathbf{p}_{e}|=|\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)|\lesssim\frac{\sigma_{N}^{3}}{\Xi(N)^{1/2}}.$
∎
Proof of Theorem 1.7.
As in the proof of Theorem 1.6, we embed the  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  into Brownian motions with drift  $\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)$ , using the stopping times  $T^{(e)}$ . We then define the  $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)$  by setting
$\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)=\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)+\varepsilon^{(e)}(t\wedge T^{(e)})$
where the  $\varepsilon^{(e)}$  are determined by  $\varepsilon^{(e)}(0)=0$  and the stochastic differential equation (4.7). We can then run the proof as in that of Theorem 1.6, using the crude estimate
$\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{N}\Big[\sup_{e}T^{(e)}>\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\Xi(N)^{3/4}\Big]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim N^{2}\left(\exp\left(-c^{\prime}\left(\frac{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\Xi(N)^{3/4}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}}\right)^{1/3}\right)+\exp\Big(-c^{\prime}\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-1/2}\Big)\right)$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}c^{\prime}\left(\frac{\Xi(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\right),$
where we used the fact that  $\Xi(N)\leq 1$  and that  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}\leq c\cdot\Xi(N)^{1/2}\log(N)^{-2}$  in the second line. Finally, the bound on  $|\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)|$  is carried out as in the previous proof, except here we are only considering one random sum of the  $T^{(f)}$ , so we use Lemma 3.7 to bound
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[\sum_{f\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})^{2}T^{(f)}>\alpha\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1}\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}\right]\lesssim\exp\left(-\tilde{c}\cdot\alpha^{1/3}\right)$
and conclude the proof from there.
∎
Remark 4.7.
Recall that assuming  $\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\lesssim R^{-1/2-c}$  allows a polynomial improvement in the corrected environment compared to the independent one. We would like to argue here that in this case, the modified variables  $(\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}$  are actually decorrelated in space, in the sense that if  $e$  and  $f$  are two edges far apart in  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$ , the variables  $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}$  and  $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{f}$  are essentially independent. We do not state or prove any result rigorous here. The variable  $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}$  can be written as  $\mathbf{p}_{e}+\varepsilon^{(e)}_{T^{(e)}}$ , and we now focus on the impact of the correction term  $\varepsilon^{(e)}_{T^{(e)}}$ , coming from the SDE (4.7). In that equation, the correlations between different  $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}$  variables come from the term  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]$ . But this term is simply a local martingale, given explicitely by Itô’s formula
$\mathrm{d}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]=\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{g}(1-\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{g})}\mathrm{Cov}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{d}B^{(g)}_{t}.$
Now assuming that some RSW property and all stability of mixing rates and events hold, the coefficient in front of  $\mathrm{d}B^{(g)}_{t}$  is of order  $\Delta_{p_{c}}(d(e,g))^{2}$ . Then the derivative of the bracket of this local martingale is of order  $\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\asymp 1$  (this last estimate assumes that  $\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\lesssim R^{-1/2-c}$ ). Furthermore, the contribution from edges  $g$  at distance at least some constant  $R$  from  $e$  to this sum is of order  $\sum_{R\leq r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\asymp R^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{4}$ , which goes to  $0$  as  $R\to\infty$ . Therefore, the local martingale  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]$  will mainly depend on edges close to  $e$ , and in the same way the local martingale  $\mathrm{d}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{f}]$  will mainly depend on edges close to  $f$ . Hence, if  $e$  and  $f$  are far apart, the process  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]$  is essentially independent of  $\mathbf{p}_{f}(t)$  and of  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{f}]$ . Plugging this back into (4.7), one gets that the processes  $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)$  and  $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{f}(t)$  are essentially independent.
5 The special case of percolation
5.1 Near-critical random bond percolation on the square lattice
Throughout this section, we will be working with  $q=1$ . We will prove Theorem 1.8 for bond percolation, first in the special case of i.i.d. Gaussian variables whose law is given by
$\mathbf{p}_{e}\overset{(d)}{=}\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{1}{2},\sigma_{N}^{2}\right),$
(5.1)
and then in the general case using once again the Skorokhod embedding theorem. The reason for treating independent bond percolation separately (i.e. separating the proofs for FK percolation of parameter  $q=1$  and the proofs for  $1<q\leq 4$  treated in Sections 3 and 4) is that the near-critical window can be extended up to  $O(\log(N)^{-2})$ , almost reaching macroscopic deformations. The previous section showed that for  $1<q\leq 4$ , one can pass from a critical window  $\textrm{W}(N,q)$ , which is expected to decay like  $N^{-\nu+o(1)}$  to near-critical random environments in the larger window  $\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N,q)^{\frac{1}{3}}=N^{-\frac{\nu}{3}+o(1)}$  with high  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$ -probability. For Bernoulli percolation, the CLE(6) conjecture implies that for  $q=1$ , the critical window is  $\textrm{W}(N,q=1)=N^{-\frac{3}{4}+o(1)}$  (which has been rigorously proven for the triangular lattice in [53, 13]). The fact that the near-critical window in a random environment is much larger comes as no surprise, as independence shows that annealed random bond percolation on a random environment where each bond variable is centred at  $p_{c}(1)=\frac{1}{2}$  has exactly the law of the critical percolation of parameter  $p_{c}(1)=\frac{1}{2}$ . Moreover, using some hands-on noise sensitivity argument, we prove in Section 5.2 that one can use even larger random variables centred at  $\frac{1}{2}$  and whose variance is is not bounded from above as  $N\to\infty$ , while keeping the large scale strong box-crossing property with high probability. Unlike the approach used up to here, this result doesn’t assert that crossing probabilities are preserved at every scale, but rather that they are preserved in the large scale regime.
In view of the next proposition, we remark that in the case of Gaussian variables  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$ , the scaling  $O(\log(N)^{-1/2})$  corresponds exactly to what is required to ensure that none of the  $N^{2}$  variables  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  leave the interval  $[0,1]$ . It is remarkable that, up to a constant factor, keeping the  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  from deviating too much from the critical value allows us to keep the RSW property at every scale, as detailed in Proposition 5.1 presented below. As we did previously, we first prove Theorem 1.8 in a simplified Gaussian case and then pass to the general case using Skorokhod embedding theorem. This reads in the following proposition.
Proposition 5.1.
Assume that  $q=1$ , and that the random environment  $(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}$  under  $\mathbf{P}_{N}$  is given by i.i.d Gaussian variables satisfying (5.1) with some uniform parameter  $\sigma_{N}$ . Then there exists some  $\delta>0$  and some  $c>0$  such that for any  $N\geq 1$ , if  $\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\log(N)^{-1/2}$ , then
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Bigg]>1-O\left(\exp\Big(-c\cdot\sigma_{N}^{-2}\Big)\right).$
We keep the notations of the previous sections and implement a similar strategy. The main reason behind the improvement from a polynomial to a logarithmic bound lies in the fact that the finite variation processes involved in Proposition 3.1 vanish for percolation due to the independence between edges. Therefore, as it represented the dominant term in the stochastic derivatives of crossings and edge influences, one should only control here the local martingale term. Set once again for  $t\geq 0$  the process  $\mathfrak{p}(t):=(\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))_{e\in E_{N}}$  formed of i.i.d Brownian motions
$\mathbf{p}_{e}(t):=p_{c}(q)+B^{(e)}_{t},$
and still denote by  $\mathcal{F}^{N}_{t}$  the naturally associated filtration. We intend to prove once again that if  $t\lesssim\log(N)$ , all the measures  $s\mapsto(\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)})_{s\leq t}$  remain within the  $\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)$  class with high probability. In the case of percolation, the independence of edges implies that the mixing rates  $\Delta^{(e)}(r)$  all vanish, making this notion irrelevant. One should therefore go back to the original study of Kesten [38] who studied the scaling relation for percolation via some refined understanding of the  $4$  arm exponent  $\pi_{4}(r)$  at each edge, which encodes the pivotality of edges. We refer to Section 2.3 where this can be explicitely seen in the estimates. Since there are no mixing rates for percolation, the breaking time  $T_{b}=T_{b}(\delta)$  is given simply by
$T_{b}:=\inf\Bigg\{t\geq 0\Bigg|\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}\not\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\cap\left(\bigcap_{\#}\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(\delta,N)\right)\Bigg\},$
where once again the intersection is taken on  $\#\in\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\textrm{rg}},3^{\textrm{lf}}\}$ . As long as  $0\leq t\leq T_{b}$ , the probability  $\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)$  that a the  $e$  is open under the measure  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}$  remains bounded away from  $0$  and  $1$ . One can once again reformulate Proposition 5.1 as the existence of some  $\delta>0$  and some  $c>0$  such that for  $\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\log(N)^{-1/2}$ ,
$\mathbf{P}\Big[T_{b}<\sigma_{N}^{2}\Big]\lesssim\exp\Big(-c\sigma_{N}^{-2}\Big).$
(5.2)
Once again, Proposition 5.1 will follow from the following lemma, which is a an adaptation of Lemma 3.3.
Lemma 5.2.
Assume that  $\delta$  is chosen small enough. There exist some positive constant  $c=c(\delta)>0$  and  $O_{\delta}$  such that if  $\sigma_{N}^{2}\leq c\cdot\log(N)^{-1}$ , one has
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall\ 0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\ \phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta}\Bigg(\exp\left(-c\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\right)\Bigg),$
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall\ 0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\ \phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\bigcap_{\#}\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(2\delta,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta}\Bigg(\exp\left(-c\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\right)\Bigg).$
Proof.
We will focus here in the proof of the first estimate, as one can adapt the proof to the second estimate as discussed at the end of the proof of Lemma 4.3. Note that we do not need the events  $\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$  and  $\mathscr{C}^{\star 1}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$  in this section as boundary conditions have no effect in percolation, so that the RSW property is given simply by estimates on the crossing events  $\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$  and  $\mathscr{C}^{\star}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$
Step 0: Canonical decomposition of the semimartingale.
Fix a  $2$  by  $1$  rectangle  $\mathcal{R}\in\mathbb{T}_{N}$ . Using the decomposition of semimartingales, one can write  $\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]=M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}+A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$  where  $M^{\mathcal{R}}$  is a local martingale started at  $0$  and  $A^{\mathcal{R}}$  is an adapted finite variation process, whose exact expression are given by
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}B^{(e)}_{t}$
$\displaystyle\mathrm{d}A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]\right)\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}t$
Step 1: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$ .
In the case of percolation, the edges parameter are independent therefore for any  $e\in E_{N}$  one has
$\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]=\mathbf{p}_{e}(t),$
and so  $\mathrm{d}A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}=0$ .
Step 2: Evaluating the order of magnitude of  $M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$ .
We estimate once again the rate of growth of the local-martingale  $M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$  via some control of its bracket, which is given by
$\mathrm{d}\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\left(\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}\right)\mathrm{d}t.$
Using again (3.3), one deduces that
$\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\asymp\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}.$
(5.3)
Now Lemma 2.14 allows us to use the critical estimates of Lemma 2.11 to get
$\forall\ 0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\quad\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\lesssim 1.$
(5.4)
Step 3: Concluding via large deviations estimates for  $M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}$ .
We conclude the proof by some straightforward large deviation estimates for the  $M^{\mathcal{R}}$  as in the previous section, we omit the details. Once again, adapting for arm events poses no difficulties.
∎
Proof of Theorem 1.8.
Once Proposition 5.1 is proven, one can apply once again the Skorokhod embedding theorem as in Section 3 to pass from Brownian motions to a sequence of general random variables satisfying  $(\star)^{q=1}_{N}$ . We simply point out the intermediate estimate which is used
$\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[\sup_{e}T^{(e)}>\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\right]\lesssim\exp(-c\cdot\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-1/2}).$
∎
5.2 Random bond percolation via noise sensitivity
The goal of this section is to extend, in the large scale limit the RSW box crossing property to deformations from the critical point which are macroscopic, meaning that one doesn’t need to scale the maximal variance  $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}$  inside  $\mathbb{T}_{N}$  to  $0$  as  $N\to\infty$ , working in true random bond context. From the previous section, this theorem comes as no surprise. Indeed, we showed that, in the case of Brownian deformations centred at the critical point, as long as the model stays critical at every scale, the stochastic derivative (5.4) is bounded independently from  $N$ . The only reason that one needs additional logarithmic factors is to brutally ensure that none of the probabilities  $\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]$  have deviated far from their original value, while one can expect that even if few boxes became too off-critical, it will not have a big influence on the criticality of the large scale model. Therefore, one should find some kind of renormalisation argument to bypass the relevance of criticality being preserved at each scale. The idea to use noise sensitivity in our context is not so surprising. In fact, the key estimate in our proof for showing that RSW holds up to windows of logarithmic size depends essentially on the estimate, for all  $2$  by  $1$  rectangles  $\mathcal{R}$ ,
$\sum_{e\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}\lesssim 1$
where we point out that the covariance is zero when  $e\not\in\mathcal{R}$ . Using half-plane two arm events (see [35, Chapter VI.1]), one can actually also show with the arguments of Section 2.3 that as the width of  $\mathcal{R}$  goes to infinity,
$\sum_{e\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}\to 0.$
(5.5)
This is exactly the usual condition used to show that the event  $\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$  is asymptotically noise sensitive as the side length of  $\mathcal{R}$  goes to infinity, see [10, Theorem 1.3]. The main difficulty with our method is that it requires that the RSW property is preserved at all scales and in all boxes, which is not enough to prove that (5.5) is preserved up to macroscopic deformations. Still, one wants to use this intuition, which hints that the missing renormalisation argument can be derived via some noise sensitivity of Bernoulli percolation, heavily studied in [10, 34, 54]. We end up using a rather hands-on argument to conclude.
Let us start with a sequence of random variables  $\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2})}$ , chosen under some probability measure  $\mathbf{P}$  such that
1.
The variables  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  are mutually independent.
2.
For each edge  $e$ , one has  $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{p}_{e}]=\frac{1}{2}$
3.
There is some  $\varepsilon>0$  such that almost surely, all of the  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  belong to  $[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]$ .
We denote by  $\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}$  the associated full-plane percolation measure. We are now in position to state the asymptotic strong box crossing property for crossings. Denote by  $S_{N}$  a square of side-length  $N$  in the plane.
Proposition 5.3.
Assume that the variables  $\mathfrak{p}$  satisfy the above conditions. Then as  $N\to\infty$ , one has the following convergence in probability
$\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{h}(S_{N})]\xlongrightarrow{(\mathbb{P})}\frac{1}{2}.$
We start by proving a particular case of the result above, which is actually just a rewording of noise sensitivity of crossing events for percolation.
Lemma 5.4 (A simple consequence of [10, 35]).
Assume  $\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon}=(\mathbf{p}_{e}^{\varepsilon})_{e}$  has the specific following law: the  $\mathbf{p}_{e}^{\varepsilon}$  are i.i.d. variables equal to  $\varepsilon$  or  $1-\varepsilon$ , each with probability  $\frac{1}{2}$ . Then the result of proposition 5.3 holds.
Proof.
Consider a realisation  $\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon}$  of the environment. We define a percolation configuration  $\mathbf{\omega}_{env}$  by setting  $\omega_{env}(e)$  to be open if  $\mathbf{p}_{e}^{\varepsilon}=1-\varepsilon$ , and closed otherwise. Note that  $\omega_{env}(e)$  is a deterministic function of the environment  $\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon}$ , but its annealed law is that of critical percolation, because each  $\mathbf{p}^{\varepsilon}_{e}$  is independently  $\varepsilon$  or  $1-\varepsilon$  with probability  $\frac{1}{2}$ .
Now consider the following way of sampling the percolation configuration  $\omega$  from the random bond percolation  $\phi_{\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon}}$ : one starts with  $\omega_{env}$ , and for each edge  $e$ , one flips the state of edge  $e$  with probability  $\varepsilon$ . Indeed, if for example  $\omega_{env}(e)=0$ , this means that  $\mathbf{p}_{e}=\varepsilon$ , and so  $\omega(e)=0=\omega_{env}(e)$  with probability  $1-\varepsilon$ , and  $\omega(e)=1=1-\omega_{env}(e)$  with probability  $\varepsilon$ , independently at each edge. Then [10, Theorem 1.2] states that the crossing events  $\mathscr{C}_{h}(S_{N})$  are asymptotically noise sensitive as  $N\to\infty$ . According to [35, Exercise IV.6], this is equivalent to saying that  $\mathbf{P}[\omega\in\mathscr{C}_{h}(S_{N})|\omega_{env}]-\mathbf{P}[\omega\in\mathscr{C}_{h}(S_{N})]$  converges to  $0$  in probability. But under the annealed probability measure  $\mathbf{P}$ ,  $\omega$  is simply a Bernoulli percolation with parameter  $\frac{1}{2}$ , so  $\mathbf{P}[\mathscr{C}_{h}(S_{N})]\to\frac{1}{2}$  as  $N\to\infty$ . This exactly gives the desired result.
∎
We now pass to the proof of Proposition 5.3 for a general set of independent random variables.
Proof.
Let  $\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2})}$  be random variables satisfying the above condition. We will write the environment  $\mathfrak{p}$  as some averaged version of the environment  $\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon}$ . Given a realisation  $\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2})}$  of the environment, one can define random variables  $(\mathbf{q}_{e})_{e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2})}$  as follows: for each edge  $e$ , take  $\mathbf{q}_{e}$  to be
$\mathbf{q}_{e}:=\begin{cases}\varepsilon&\text{ with probability }\frac{1-\varepsilon-\mathbf{p}_{e}}{1-2\varepsilon}\\
1-\varepsilon&\text{ with probability }\frac{\mathbf{p}_{e}-\varepsilon}{1-2\varepsilon},\end{cases}$
in a way that the variables  $\mathbf{q}_{e}$  are independent, both unconditionally and conditionally on  $\mathfrak{p}$ . Note that this definition makes sense precisely because  $\mathbf{p}_{e}$  is almost surely in  $[\varepsilon;1-\varepsilon]$ , and it is straightforward to see that  $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{q}_{e}|\mathfrak{p}]=\mathbf{p}_{e}$ . Consider the random environment  $\mathfrak{q}=(\mathbf{q}_{e})_{e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2})}$ . Not conditioning anymore on the random variables  $\mathfrak{p}$ , this environment  $\mathfrak{q}$  has independent bonds taking values in  $\{\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon\}$ , and it satisfies, for each  $e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2})$ ,  $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{q}_{e}]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{q}_{e}|\mathfrak{p}]]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{p}_{e}]=\frac{1}{2}$ . Therefore,  $\mathfrak{q}$  actually has the law of the environment  $\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon}$  given in Lemma 5.4. This allows to conclude that for any  $\gamma>0$ ,
$\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|>\gamma\Bigg]\underset{N\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0,$
which, by Markov’s inequality, implies that
$\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|>\gamma\ \Bigg|\mathfrak{p}\Bigg]>\gamma\Bigg]\underset{N\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0.$
To conclude, it is enough to notice that to sample the percolation configuration  $\omega$  under  $\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}$ , one can first sample  $\mathfrak{q}$  from  $\mathfrak{p}$ , and then sample  $\omega$  from  $\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}$  (as  $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{q}_{e}|\mathfrak{p}]=\mathbf{p}_{e}$ ). Therefore
$\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]|\mathfrak{p}],$
which allows to write
$\displaystyle\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|$
$\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|\ \Bigg|\mathfrak{p}\Bigg]$
$\displaystyle\leq\gamma+\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|>\gamma\ \Bigg|\mathfrak{p}\Bigg].$
This allows to conclude that
$\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|>2\gamma\Bigg]\leq\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|>\gamma\ \Bigg|\mathfrak{p}\Bigg]>\gamma\Bigg]\underset{N\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0.$
This concludes the proof.
∎
Let us now move on to proving that Cardy’s formula stays true in a random environment.
Proof of Theorem 1.10.
Fix some  $x\in[0,1]$ , and consider the crossing event denoted  $F_{N}(x)=\mathcal{C}([C_{N};A_{N}],[x_{N};B_{N}])$ . If  $x=0$  or  $x=1$ , then  $\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)]$  is identically  $0$  or  $1$  respectively. Assuming that  $x\in(0,1)$ , we claim that as  $N\to\infty$ , the events  $F_{N}(x)$  are asymptotically noise-sensitive. Indeed, one can follow the same computations as in [35, Chapter VI.1] by considering the quadrilateral  $A_{N}B_{N}x_{N}C_{N}$ . The key point is that all of the sides of this quadrilateral are straight lines, so one can use half-plane three arm events, and the corners have an opening angle of  $\pi$  at  $x_{N}$  and  $\pi/3\leq\pi$  at  $A_{N},B_{N},C_{N}$  (see Figure 1 in the introduction), so one can use half-plane two arm events to control pivotality in the corners. Then one can run the proof of Proposition 5.3 to get that as  $N\to\infty$ ,
$\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)]-\mathbf{P}[F_{N}(x)]\xlongrightarrow{(\mathbb{P})}0.$
Once again, the annealed model is simply critical Bernoulli percolation, which ensures via Theorem 1.9 that one has  $\mathbb{P}[F_{N}(x)]\to 1-x$  as  $N\to\infty$ . Therefore, one gets that  $\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)]$  converges to  $1-x$  in probability as  $N\to\infty$ .
Now we quickly explain how to pass from this “pointwise” convergence in probability to the “uniform” convergence in probability of Theorem 1.10. This is a basic consequence of the fact that the  $x\mapsto\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)]$  are increasing. Indeed, fix some  $K$  and consider  $x_{i}=\frac{i}{K}$  for  $i=0,1,\ldots,K$ . We may take  $N$  large enough so that for each  $i$ , one has
$\mathbf{P}\big[|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x_{i})]-x_{i}|>1/K\big]\leq\frac{1}{K(K+1)}.$
so that by a union bound,
$\mathbf{P}\big[\forall\ 0\leq i\leq K,\quad|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x_{i})]-x_{i}|\leq 1/K\big]>1-1/K.$
Under this event, for each  $x\in(0,1)$ , let  $i$  be the index such that  $x_{i}\leq x<x_{i+1}$ . Then we may write
$x_{i}-1/K\leq\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x_{i})]\leq\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)]\leq\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x_{i+1})]\leq x_{i+1}+1/K.$
Plugging in the fact that  $x_{i+1}\leq x+1/K$  and  $x_{i}\geq x-1/K$  gives that  ${|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)]-x|\leq 2/K}$ . Therefore, for  $N$  large enough,
$\mathbf{P}\big[\forall\ x\in[0,1],\quad|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)]-x|\leq 2/K\big]>1-1/K$
Taking  $N\to\infty$  and  $K\to\infty$  sufficiently slowly gives exactly the statement of Theorem 1.10.
∎
Appendix A Computations
A.1 Derivatives in the  $p_{e}$  in non translation invariant environments
We prove now Proposition 2.13 which generalises the formulae used extensively in [25] when differentiating the probability of an event with respect to some uniform parameter  $p$ , which is in our context no longer the same at each edge. All results in this section are valid on general graphs  $G=(V,E)$  and for all  $q$ , so we will ignore all dependencies on the graph and on  $q$ . Recall the weight of a configuration  $w_{\underline{p}}(\omega)$  whose expression is given just above the statement of Proposition 2.13.
Proof of Proposition 2.13.
First, using the formula for  $w_{\underline{p}}(\omega)$ , we may write, for all edges  $e\in E_{N}$  and all  $\omega$
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}w_{\underline{p}}(\omega)$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})}\mathbbm{1}(\omega_{e}=1)w_{\underline{p}}(\omega),$
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{e}^{2}}w_{\underline{p}}(\omega)$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})^{2}}\mathbbm{1}(\omega_{e}=1)w_{\underline{p}}(\omega).$
For an event  $\mathcal{S}$ , one can write directly that
$\phi_{\underline{p}}[\mathcal{S}]=\frac{Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S})}{Z_{\underline{p}}},\quad\textrm{ with }Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S}):=\sum_{\omega\in\mathcal{S}}w_{\underline{p}}(\omega)$
(A.1)
and  $Z_{\underline{p}}=Z_{\underline{p}}(\{0,1\}^{E})$  is the partition function of the model. For any edge  $e\in E_{N}$ , plugging in the expressions for the derivatives of  $w_{\underline{p}}(\omega)$  gives
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S})$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})}Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S}\cap\{\omega_{e}=1\}),$
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{e}^{2}}Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S})$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})^{2}}Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S}\cap\{\omega_{e}=1\}).$
In particular
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\mathcal{S}]$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z_{\underline{p}}}\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S})-\frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}Z_{\underline{p}}}{Z_{\underline{p}}^{2}}Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S})$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})}\left[\frac{1}{Z_{\underline{p}}}Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S}\cap\{\omega_{e}=1\})-\frac{Z_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e}=1)}{Z_{\underline{p}}^{2}}Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S})\right]$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})}\Big[\phi_{\underline{p}}[\mathcal{S}\cap\{\omega_{e}=1\}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\phi[\mathcal{S}]\Big]$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})}\textrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e}).$
As a corollary, one deduces that for any edges  $e_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{n},f$ , not necessarily distinct, one has
$\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{f}}\phi_{\underline{p}}\left[\prod_{k=1}^{n}\omega_{e_{i}}\right]=\frac{1}{p_{f}(1-p_{f})}\left(\phi_{\underline{p}}\left[\omega_{f}\prod_{k=1}^{n}\omega_{e_{i}}\right]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]\phi_{\underline{p}}\left[\prod_{k=1}^{n}\omega_{e_{i}}\right]\right).$
Applying this to  $\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})=\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}\omega_{f}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]$ , one gets for any  $e,f,g\in E_{N}$ ,
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{g}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{g}(1-p_{g})}\Bigg(\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}\omega_{e}\omega_{f}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}\omega_{f}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}\omega_{f}]$
$\displaystyle\quad+\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}\omega_{e}]+\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\Bigg)$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{g}(1-p_{g})}\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g)$
We compute now the second derivatives of  $\phi_{\underline{p}}[\mathcal{S}]$ .
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{e}^{2}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\mathcal{S}]$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z_{\underline{p}}}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{e}^{2}}Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S})-2\frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}Z_{\underline{p}}}{Z_{\underline{p}}^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S})+\frac{-Z_{\underline{p}}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{e}^{2}}Z_{\underline{p}}+2(\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}Z_{\underline{p}})^{2}}{Z_{\underline{p}}^{3}}Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S})$
$\displaystyle=\frac{2}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})^{2}}\frac{Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S}\cap\{\omega_{e}=1\})}{Z_{\underline{p}}}-\frac{2}{p_{e}^{2}(1-p_{e})^{2}}\frac{Z_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e}=1)}{Z_{\underline{p}}}\frac{Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S}\cap\{\omega_{e}=1\})}{Z_{\underline{p}}}$
$\displaystyle\quad-\frac{2}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})^{2}}\frac{Z_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e}=1)}{Z_{\underline{p}}}\frac{Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S})}{Z_{\underline{p}}}+\frac{2}{p_{e}^{2}(1-p_{e})^{2}}\frac{Z_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e}=1)^{2}}{Z_{\underline{p}}^{2}}\frac{Z_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S})}{Z_{\underline{p}}}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{2}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p_{e}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\right)\textrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e}).$
And now differentiating twice covariances with respect to an edge bond  $p_{g}$ :
$\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{g}^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})$
$\displaystyle=\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{g}^{2}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}\omega_{f}]-\left(\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{g}^{2}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\right)\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\left(\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial p_{g}^{2}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]\right)$
$\displaystyle\hskip 113.81102pt-2\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{g}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\right)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{g}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]\right)$
$\displaystyle=\frac{2}{p_{g}(1-p_{g})^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p_{g}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\right)\Big[\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}\omega_{f}\omega_{g}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}\omega_{f}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\Big]$
$\displaystyle\quad-\frac{2}{p_{g}(1-p_{g})^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p_{g}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\right)\Big[\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}\omega_{g}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\Big]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]$
$\displaystyle\quad-\frac{2}{p_{g}(1-p_{g})^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p_{g}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\right)\Big[\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}\omega_{g}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\Big]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]$
$\displaystyle\quad-\frac{2}{p_{g}^{2}(1-p_{g})^{2}}\Big[\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}\omega_{g}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{e}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\Big]\Big[\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}\omega_{g}]-\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{f}]\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\Big]$
$\displaystyle=\frac{2}{p_{g}(1-p_{g})^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p_{g}}\phi_{\underline{p}}[\omega_{g}]\right)\kappa_{3}^{\underline{p}}(e,f,g)$
$\displaystyle\quad-\frac{2}{p_{g}^{2}(1-p_{g})^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{f},\omega_{g}).$
∎
We mention that the computations of the first derivatives can be seen as a special case of the following more general result on cumulants of events. Since we will not be needing this result, we do not recall the definition of cumulants and we skip its proof.
Lemma A.1.
Let  $A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{n}$  be events, and let  $e\in E_{N}$  be an edge. Then one has the identity for all  $\underline{p}$ :
$\frac{\partial}{\partial p_{e}}\kappa^{\underline{p}}_{n}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{n})=\frac{1}{p_{e}(1-p_{e})}\kappa^{\underline{p}}_{n+1}(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{n},\omega_{e}).$
A.2 Proofs of crossing estimates via arm events
We collect here the proofs of geometric estimates stated in Section 2.3. In these proofs, we do not detail the geometric estimates based on RSW, and for the sake of readability, we will often identify lengths at the same scale, for example instead of writing “there is a four-arm event from scales  $2r$  to  $R/2$ ”, we would write “there is a four-arm event from scales  $r$  to  $R$ ”.
Proof of Lemma 2.7.
The first item was already derived in [25], therefore we focus on the second item. Let  $e$  be an edge at distance  $n\lesssim R$  from the corners of  $\mathcal{R}$  and set  $\ell=\textrm{dist}(e,\partial\mathcal{R})$ . According to [25, Lemma 5.3], one may write
$\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\lesssim\sum_{r=1}^{3R}\frac{\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)}{r}\phi_{p_{c}}[\textrm{Piv}_{r,e}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}))]$
where for an event  $\mathcal{S}$ ,  $\textrm{Piv}_{r,e}(\mathcal{S})$  is the event that the event that  $\mathcal{S}$  holds and that the box  $\Lambda_{r}(e)$  is pivotal for the event  $\mathcal{S}$ . To conclude, one should evaluate  $\phi_{p_{c}}[\textrm{Piv}_{r,e}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}))]$ , which is done by dichotomy on the value of  $r$ . We refer to Figure 4 for an illustration of the following cases. Since there is no risk of confusion, we will not write the subscript  $p_{c}$  for  $\Delta,\pi_{4},\pi_{3^{+}}$  in this proof.
•
Case 1:  $n\leq r\leq 3R$ . The pivotality event  $\textrm{Piv}_{r,e}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}))$  implies the existence of two arms, of different parity, going from  $\Lambda_{r}(e)$  to a distance  $R$  inside of  $\mathcal{R}$ . By standard RSW estimates, the probability of the latter decays polynomially fast, at a speed  $\lesssim(r/R)^{c}$  for some  $c>0$ .
•
Case 2:  $\ell\leq r\leq n$ . The pivotality event implies the existence of  $3$  arms of alternating parity going from  $\Lambda_{r}(e)$  to distance  $n$  in  $\mathcal{R}$ , and together with two arms of different parity going from  $\Lambda_{n}(e)$  to distance  $R$  in  $\mathcal{R}$ . Therefore, Remark 2.6 together with standard RSW estimates ensures that the pivotality event happens with probability at most  $(r/n)^{2}(n/R)^{c}$  for some  $c=c(\delta)>0$ .
•
Case 3:  $r\leq\ell$ . The pivotality event implies existence of four alternating parity arms from  $\Lambda_{r}(e)$  to distance  $\ell$ , together with three alternating parity arms from  $\Lambda_{\ell}(e)$  to distance  $n$  in  $\mathcal{R}$ , and finally two alternating arms from  $\Lambda_{n}(e)$  to distance  $R$  in  $\mathcal{R}$ . Using again Remark 2.6 and RSW, the pivotality event happens with probability at most  $\pi_{4}(r,\ell)(\ell/n)^{2}(n/R)^{c}$ .
Figure 4: An illustration of the pivotality event  $\textrm{Piv}_{r,e}(\mathscr{C}_{h}(\mathcal{R}))$  in the three cases explicited in the proof. In these figures, all distances denoted by  $r,n,\ell$  are to be understood as being of order  $r,n,\ell$ , and  $\mathcal{R}$  is represented as a square. We only illustrate the case where  $e$  is inside  $\mathcal{R}$  but the case when  $e$  is outside is analogous.
This implies that
$\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}\frac{\Delta(r)}{r}\pi_{4}(r,\ell)(\ell/n)^{2}(n/R)^{c}+\sum_{r=\ell}^{n}\frac{\Delta(r)}{r}(r/n)^{2}(n/R)^{c}+\sum_{r=n}^{R}\frac{\Delta(r)}{r}(r/R)^{c}$
$\displaystyle\asymp\frac{\ell^{2}\Delta(\ell)}{n^{2-c}R^{c}}\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}\frac{\pi_{4}(r,\ell)}{r\Delta(r,\ell)}+\frac{1}{n^{2-c}R^{c}}\sum_{r=\ell}^{n}r\Delta(r)+\frac{1}{R^{c}}\sum_{r=n}^{R}\frac{\Delta(r)}{r^{1+c}}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\frac{\ell^{2}\Delta(\ell)}{n^{2-c}R^{c}}+\frac{n^{c}}{R^{c}}\Delta(n)+\Delta(n)\lesssim\Delta(n).$
Passing from the second to the third line, we used Remark 2.6 by writing
•
In the first sum,  $\frac{\pi_{4}(r,\ell)}{\Delta(r,\ell)}\lesssim(r/\ell)^{-c}$ .
•
In the second sum,  $\sum_{r=\ell}^{n}r\Delta(r)\lesssim n^{2}\Delta(n)$  as  $\Delta(r,n)\gtrsim(r/n)^{2-c}$ .
•
In the third sum  $\Delta(r)\leq\Delta(n)$  for  $r\geq n$ .
The last inequality uses that  $\ell^{2}\Delta(\ell)\lesssim n^{2}\Delta(n)$  for  $\ell\leq n$  and that  $n\leq R$ .
∎
Sketch of proof of Lemma 2.9.
We sketch the proof for  $\#=3^{+}$ , the case  $\#=4$  is analogous (and even simpler). One again one has
$\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathcal{A}_{3^{+}}^{(e)}(R),\omega_{f})\lesssim\sum_{r=1}^{R}\frac{\Delta(r)}{r}\phi_{p_{c}}[\textrm{Piv}_{r,f}(\mathcal{A}_{3^{+}}^{(e)}(R))]$
Recall (as it was not relevant for the proof of Lemma 2.7) that the event  $\textrm{Piv}_{r,f}(\mathcal{A}_{3^{+}}^{(e)}(R))$  not only requires that the box  $\Lambda_{r}(f)$  is pivotal for the arm event, but also that the associated arm event itself holds, bringing an additional multiplicative factor of small probability. We run once again a dichotomy, depending on the position of  $f$ , encoded by  $n$ , and  $\ell$ , the distance from  $f$  to the boundary of the half-plane centred at  $e$ . This implies that  $n\leq\ell$ . We now estimate  $\phi_{p_{c}}[\textrm{Piv}_{r,f}(\mathcal{A}_{3^{+}}^{(e)}(R))]$  depending on  $r$  with respect to  $\ell$  and  $n$ . See Figure 5 for an illustration of the following cases. Once again, we do not write the subscript  $p_{c}$  in this proof.
•
Case 1:  $r\geq n$ . One can crudely bound  $\phi_{p_{c}}[\textrm{Piv}_{r,f}(\mathcal{A}_{3^{+}}^{(e)}(R))]$  by the probability of  $\mathcal{A}_{3^{+}}^{(e)}(R)$  arm event, which is (up to constant)  $\pi_{3^{+}}(R)$ . This bound is sharp (up to constant) when  $f$  is at distance at most  $r$  from  $e$ .
•
Case 2:  $\ell\leq r\leq n$  while  $n=d(e,f)$ . In that case, the pivotality of  $f$  at scale  $r$  implies the existence of a half-plane three arm event from  $\Lambda_{r}(f)$  to distance  $\ell$ , together with some half-plane three arm event to scale  $n$  from  $e$ , and a half-plane three arm event from scales  $n$  to scale  $R$  around  $e$  and  $f$ . Therefore, one can bound the probability of the pivotality by  $\pi_{3^{+}}(r,n)\pi_{3^{+}}(n)\pi_{3^{+}}(n,R)$ .
•
Case 3:  $\ell\leq r\leq n$  while  $n$  is the distance from  $f$  to one of the bottom corners of  $\Lambda_{R}(e)\cap\mathbb{H}^{(e)}_{N}$ . Then the pivotality event implies some half-plane three arm event from  $\Lambda_{r}(f)$  to distance  $n$ , together with a half-plane three arm event from  $e$  to distance  $R$ . Therefore, one can upper bound the probability of the pivotality by  $\pi_{3^{+}}(r,n)\pi_{3^{+}}(R)$ . By quasi-multiplicativity, this bound is of the same order of magnitude as the one of Case  $2$ . Notice that this is of the same order as the previous case.
•
Case 4:  $r\leq\ell$ . In that case, the pivotality implies the existence a four-arm event from  $\Lambda_{r}(f)$  up to distance  $\ell$ , together with the event described in case  $3$ , replacing  $r$  by  $\ell$ . One can then bounds the pivotality probability by  $\pi_{4}(r,\ell)\pi_{3^{+}}(\ell,n)\pi_{3^{+}}(n)\pi_{3^{+}}(n,R)$ .
Figure 5: An illustration of the four cases in the proof. Once again, any length denoted by  $r,n,\ell$  is to be understood as being of order  $r,n,\ell$  (see figure of Case  $2$  where two different lengths are denoted  $n$ ). The greyed out parts in Cases  $2$  and  $4$  and the darker path in Case  $3$  are not taken into account in the upper bound on the probability of being pivotal.
Putting everything together and using quasi-multiplicativity, one gets
$\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathcal{A}_{3^{+}}^{(e)}(R),\omega_{f})$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}\frac{\Delta(r)}{r}\pi_{4}(r,\ell)\pi_{3^{+}}(\ell,n)\pi_{3^{+}}(n)\pi_{3^{+}}(n,R)$
$\displaystyle+\sum_{r=\ell}^{n}\frac{\Delta(r)}{r}\pi_{3^{+}}(r,n)\pi_{3^{+}}(n)\pi_{3^{+}}(n,R)+\sum_{r=n}^{R}\frac{\Delta(r)}{r}\pi_{3^{+}}(R).$
This allows to conclude that
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{\pi_{3^{+}}(R)}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathcal{A}_{3^{+}}^{(e)}(R),\omega_{f})$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}\frac{\Delta(r)}{r}\pi_{4}(r,\ell)\pi_{3^{+}}(\ell,n)+\sum_{r=\ell}^{n}\frac{\Delta(r)}{r}\pi_{3^{+}}(r,n)+\sum_{r=n}^{R}\frac{\Delta(r)}{r}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\Delta(\ell)+\Delta(\ell)+\Delta(\ell),$
where passing to the last line one uses the existence of  $c>0$  (see Remark 2.6) such that
•
$\pi_{3^{+}}(d,\ell)\lesssim\Delta(d,\ell)(d/\ell)^{c}$  and  $\pi_{4}(r,d)\lesssim\Delta(r,d)(r/d)^{c}$  in the first sum.
•
$\pi_{3^{+}}(r,\ell)\asymp(r/\ell)^{2}\lesssim\Delta(r,\ell)(r/\ell)^{c}$  in the second sum.
•
$\Delta(r)\lesssim\Delta(\ell)(\ell/r)^{c}$  for the last sum.
This concludes the proof.
∎
Proof of Lemma 2.11 in the case of crossing events.
In the case of percolation, one may rewrite
$\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\asymp\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p_{c},1}[\textrm{Piv}_{e}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}))]$
where  $\textrm{Piv}_{e}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}))$  is the event that  $e$  is pivotal for the event  $\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$ . Note that if  $e$  does not belong to  $\mathcal{R}$ , this probability is simply  $0$ . Assume now that  $e$  belongs to  $\mathcal{R}$ , and let  $\ell\leq n$  be respectively the distance from  $e$  to  $\partial\mathcal{R}$  and from  $e$  to a corner of  $\mathcal{R}$ .
