The event that  $e$  is pivotal for  $\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})$  implies the existence of a four-arm event around  $e$  from scales  $1$  to  $\ell$ , then a half-plane three arm event from scales  $\ell$  to  $n$ , and finally a quarter-plane two arm event from scales  $n$  to  $1$ . This is exactly what is depicted in Figure 4 when setting  $r=1$ . By point (iv) of Remark 2.6 (lower bound) there exists a constant  $c>0$  such that
$\displaystyle\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p_{c},1}[\textrm{Piv}_{e}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}))]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\pi_{4}(\ell)\pi_{3^{+}}(\ell,n)\lesssim\pi_{4}(\ell)(\ell/n)^{2}\lesssim\pi_{4,p_{c}}(n),$
where we once again choose to not write the subscripts  $p_{c}$ . Summing over all edges  $e\in\mathcal{R}$  gives, using point (iv) of Remark 2.6 (lower bound)
$\displaystyle\sum_{e\in\mathcal{R}}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{n}n\cdot\pi_{4}(n)\asymp\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}.$
Finally, using the upper bound of the fourth item of Remark 2.6, one gets
$\displaystyle\sum_{e\in\mathcal{R}}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{n}n\cdot\pi_{4}(n)^{2}\asymp 1.$
∎
Proof of Lemma 2.12.
For this proof, we recall that the scaling relations ensures that one has  $\textrm{W}(N)\asymp N^{-2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(N)^{-1}\asymp(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r))^{-1}$ . The inequality on the left without the polynomial improvement comes from the trivial bound  $\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\lesssim\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)$ , which is of order  $\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}$ . In order to get the polynomial improvement, we recall the inequality  $(r/R)^{c}\gtrsim\Delta_{p_{c}}(r,R)\asymp\frac{\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)}{\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)}\gtrsim(r/R)^{2-c}$  for some  $c>0$ , which allows us to write
$\displaystyle\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}$
$\displaystyle\leq\sum_{r\leq\sqrt{N}}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)+\Delta_{p_{c}}\left(\sqrt{N}\right)^{3}\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\left(\sqrt{N}\right)^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}\left(\sqrt{N}\right)+\left(\sqrt{N}\right)^{-3c}\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\left(\sqrt{N}/N\right)^{-c}N^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(N)+\left(\sqrt{N}\right)^{-3c}\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}$
$\displaystyle\lesssim N^{-c/2}\textrm{W}(N)^{-1},$
where in the second to last line, we used that  $\textrm{W}(N)^{-1}\asymp N^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(N)$ . Plugging this into the expression of  $\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)$  gives the first inequality of the lemma with constant  $c/6$ . For the inequality on the right, simply rearranging the terms shows that it is equivalent to
$\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2}\lesssim\left(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)\right)^{2/3}\left(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\right)^{1/3},$
which is just the Hölder inequality applied to  $r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2}=(r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r))^{2/3}(r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4})^{1/3}$ .
∎
Appendix B Estimates on Skorokhod embedding stopping times
B.1 Tails for Skorokhod embedding stopping times
In this section, we prove Lemma 3.6. We point out that when the random variable  $X$  is bounded, there are simpler arguments that show that  $T$  has exponential tails (which is the case  $\gamma=\infty$ ).
Proof of Lemma 3.6.
The goal will be to use the so-called Vallois embedding [55] in order to construct some stopping time  $T$  adapted to a standard Brownian motion  $(B_{t})_{t\geq 0}$  such that  $B_{T}\overset{(d)}{=}X$ . We denote  $\mathcal{F}_{t}:=\sigma\Big(B_{s},0\leq s\leq t\Big)$  the naturally associated filtration. Let us recall explicitly this construction here, which corresponds to [17] in the special case where  $h(s)=s$  and  $F=0$ . We mostly keep the notations of [17] in order to simplify cross-reading between the articles. All the constants involved in the statements depend only on  $c$  and  $\gamma$ . Let  $\mu$  be the law of the random variable  $X$  and set for  $x\in\mathbb{R}$  its potential denoted  $U_{\mu}(x)$  (which is related to the function  $c(x)$  in [17]) and given by
$U_{\mu}(x):=-\int_{\mathbb{R}}|x-y|d\mu(y)=-x-2\int_{x}^{\infty}(y-x)d\mu(y).$
This allows to define the functions  $\theta,\phi,R,S,\Gamma$  as:
$\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\theta(s):=\textrm{argmin}_{x>0}\left\{\frac{-s-U_{\mu}(x)}{x}\right\},\\
\phi(s):=\textrm{argmax}_{x<0}\left\{\frac{-s-U_{\mu}(x)}{x}\right\},\end{array}\right.\quad\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}R(s):=\frac{-s-U_{\mu}(\theta(s))}{\theta(s)},\\
S(s):=\frac{-s-U_{\mu}(\phi(s))}{\phi(s)},\\
\Gamma(s):=\frac{R(s)-S(s)}{2}.\end{array}\right.$
One can then parametrize the time using  $H(s):=\int_{0}^{s}\frac{dz}{\Gamma(z)}$  and define the reparametrized versions of  $\theta$  and  $\phi$  by setting:
$a(\ell):=\theta(H^{-1}(\ell)),\quad b(\ell):=\phi(H^{-1}(\ell)).$
Let  $L_{t}$  be the local time of  $B_{t}$  at  $0$  [40]. The Vallois stopping time [55] is given by [17, Equation (2)] to the filtration  $\mathcal{F}_{t}$  and is defined by
$T_{V}:=\inf\{t\geq 0|B_{t}\not\in(b(L_{t}),a(L_{t}))\}.$
(B.1)
The main goal of this section is to obtain tail estimates for the variable  $T_{V}$ . In order to simplify the reading, we assume that the law  $\mu$  has a density with respect to the Lebesgue measure (denoted here by  $f$ ), but the announced results hold in full generality. Given the formulation  $\theta(s)$  as an argmax on  $\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}$ , it is straightforward to see that
$\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\frac{-s-U_{\mu}(x)}{x}\right)|_{x=\theta(s)}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\frac{-s+2\int_{x}^{\infty}(y-x)f(y)dy}{x}+1\right)|_{x=\theta(s)}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{s-2\int_{\theta(s)}^{\infty}yf(y)dy}{\theta(s)^{2}}=0,$
which ensures that
$s=2\int_{\theta(s)}^{\infty}yf(y)dy\lesssim\exp(-c\cdot\theta(s)^{\gamma}).$
The above equation reads as  $\theta(s)\lesssim\log(1/s)^{1/\gamma}$ , and the same estimate holds by symmetry for  $-\phi(s)$ . This ensures that as long as  $s$  remains far away from  $0$  and  $\infty$ , both functions  $\theta,-\phi$  remain also bounded away from  $0$  and  $\infty$ . In order to finish the proof, one needs to estimate all three functions  $R,S,\Gamma$  in the  $s\to 0$  regime. One has
$\displaystyle R(s)$
$\displaystyle=\frac{-s-U_{\mu}(\theta(s))}{\theta(s)}=\frac{\theta(s)+\int_{\theta(s)}^{\infty}(2(y-\theta(s))-2y)f(y)dy}{\theta(s)}$
$\displaystyle=1-2\mu[\theta(s),\infty).$
Similarly one gets that  $S(s)=-1-2\mu(-\infty,\phi(s)]$  and therefore
$\Gamma(s)=1-\big(\mu[\theta(s),\infty)-\mu(-\infty,\phi(s)]\big).$
It is clear from the definitions of  $\theta(s)$  and  $\phi(s)$  that when  $s\to 0$ , the functions  $\theta(s),-\phi(s)$  diverge to  $+\infty$ , which ensure that  $\Gamma$  is bounded from below and  $H(s)$  grows at linear speed when  $s\to 0$ . This ensures that for  $\ell>0$  small enough, the functions  $a(\ell)$  and  $b(\ell)$  satisfy
$a(\ell),-b(\ell)\lesssim\log(1/\ell)^{1/\gamma}.$
When  $\ell\gtrsim 1$ , we simply bound  $a(\ell),b(\ell)$  by some constant  $C>0$ . Then  $T_{V}$  is bounded by the stopping time  $\inf\{t|B_{t}\not\in(-C,C)\}$  which has exponential tails, plus the stopping time  $T^{*}$  defined by
$T^{*}:=\inf\big\{t\geq 0\big||B_{t}|\geq C\log(1/L_{t})^{1/\gamma}\big\}$
Fix some  $\varepsilon>0$  (which will be adjusted later in the proof). Using the union bound, for any  $t>0$ , one can write
$\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big[T^{*}>t\Big]$
$\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\Big[T^{*}>t,L_{t/2}>\varepsilon\Big]+\mathbb{P}\Big[T^{*}>t,L_{t/2}\leq\varepsilon\Big]$
$\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left[\sup_{s\leq t/2}|B_{s}|<2\log(1/\varepsilon)^{1/\gamma}\right]+\mathbb{P}\Big[L_{t/2}\leq\varepsilon\Big]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left(\frac{-c}{\log(1/\varepsilon)^{2/\gamma}}t\right)+\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{t}}.$
Set  $\varepsilon=\exp\left(-t^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\right)$ , which ensures that for  $t\gtrsim 1$  one has, for  $c>0$  small enough,
$\mathbb{P}\Big[T_{V}>t\Big]\lesssim\mathbb{P}\Big[T^{*}>t/2\Big]+\exp(-ct)\lesssim\exp\left(-ct^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\right),$
since  $\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}\leq 1$ , which concludes the proof.
∎
B.2 Tails for Skorokhod embedding stopping times with drift
In this section, we prove Lemma 4.5. Once again, when  $X$  is bounded, one may show that the result holds with  $\gamma=\infty$ .
Proof of Lemma 4.5.
Set  $Y_{t}=B_{t}-\mu t$ . From the process  $(Y_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ , one can naturally construct a martingale  $Z_{t}=e^{2\mu Y_{t}}-1$  such that  $Z_{0}=0$  almost surely. The Dubins-Schwarz Theorem ensures the existence of a Brownian motion  $\widetilde{B}$  adapted to some modified filtration (potentially defined on some extended probability space), such that  $Z_{t}=\widetilde{B}_{\langle Z,Z\rangle_{t}}$ . Applying the Skorokhod embedding theorem recalled above to the centred random variable  $e^{2\mu X}-1$ , there exists some stopping time  $T_{V}$  such that  $\widetilde{B}_{T_{V}}\overset{(d)}{=}e^{2\mu X}-1$ . One can then define the stopping time
$T:=\inf\{t\geq 0|\langle Z,Z\rangle_{t}=T_{V}\}.$
Let us see why this  $T$  satisfies the first condition of the lemma. One can couple  $(Y,\widetilde{B},T_{V})$  to  $X$  in such a way that  $\widetilde{B}_{T_{V}}=e^{2\mu X}-1$ . Then one may write, on the event that  $\{T<\infty\}$ ,
$e^{2\mu X}-1=\widetilde{B}_{T_{V}}=\widetilde{B}_{\langle Z,Z\rangle_{T}}=Z_{T}=e^{2\mu Y_{T}}-1$
Since  $x\mapsto e^{2\mu X}-1$  is injective, one gets that  $X=Y_{T}$  on the event  $\{T<\infty\}$ .
Given the definition of  $T$ , it is not mandatory that  $\langle Z,Z\rangle_{t}\to\infty$  as  $t\to\infty$ , therefore the event  $\{T=\infty\}$  may happen with positive probability. Still, in the regime  $\sigma\ll 1$  which is relevant in our setup, this will happen with a small probability depending on  $\sigma$ . Fix some parameter  $\varepsilon\ll 1$ , whose value will be fixed later in the reasoning. In order to estimate the tail of the stopping time  $T$ , one can make the dichotomy
$\mathbb{P}\Big[T>t\Big]\leq\mathbb{P}\Big[T_{V}>\mu t\Big]+\mathbb{P}\Big[T>T_{V}/\mu,T_{V}\leq\mu t\Big].$
(B.2)
Combining the fact that  $|X|\leq 1$  and that  $\mu$  is bounded away from  $0$  and  $\infty$  ensures that  $e^{2\mu X}-1$  also has the same stretched exponential tail as  $X$ . Therefore
$\mathbb{P}\Big[T_{V}>\mu t\Big]\lesssim\exp\Big(-c^{\prime}\cdot\Big(\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}}\Big)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\Big)$
for some constant  $c^{\prime}$  only depending on  $c$ . In order to derive tails bounds for the the stopping time  $T$ , it remains to evaluate the second term in the RSH of (B.2). One has
$\mathbb{P}\Big[T>T_{V}/\mu,T_{V}\leq\mu t\Big]=\mathbb{P}\Big[\langle Z,Z\rangle_{T_{V}/\mu}<T_{V},T_{V}\leq\mu t\Big]$
Computing explicitly the bracket of  $Z$ , one gets
$\langle Z,Z\rangle_{T_{V}/\mu}=2\mu\int_{0}^{T_{V}/\mu}e^{2\mu Y_{t}}\mathrm{d}t\geq 2T_{V}\cdot\exp\Big(2\mu\Big(\inf_{0\leq s\leq T_{V}/\mu}Y_{s}\Big)\Big).$
Let  $\mu_{T_{V}}$  be the law of the stopping time  $T_{V}$ . The previous equation
implies that
$\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big[\langle Z,Z\rangle_{T_{V}/\mu}<T_{V},T_{V}\leq\mu t\Big]$
$\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left[\inf_{0\leq s\leq T_{V}/\mu}Y_{s}<-\frac{\log 2}{2\mu},T_{V}\leq\mu t\right]$
$\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\mu t}\mathbb{P}\left[\inf_{0\leq s\leq u/\mu}Y_{s}<-\frac{\log 2}{2\mu}\right]d\mu_{T_{V}}(u)$
$\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{\mu t}\mathbb{P}\left[\inf_{0\leq s\leq u/\mu}B_{s}<u-\frac{\log 2}{2\mu}\right]d\mu_{T_{V}}(u).$
Assuming that  $t$  is chosen smaller than some constant depending on  $\mu$ , and that  $\mu t$  is not an atom of  $\mu_{T_{V}}$ , there exist  $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}>0$ , only depending on  $c,\gamma,\mu$  such that
$\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\mu t}\mathbb{P}\left[\inf_{0\leq s\leq u/\mu}B_{s}<u-\frac{\log 2}{2\mu}\right]d\mu_{T_{V}}(u)$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\int_{0}^{\mu t}\exp\Big(-\frac{c_{1}}{u}\Big)d\mu_{T_{V}}(u)$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\Bigg(\int_{0}^{\mu t}\exp\Big(-\frac{c_{2}}{u}-c_{2}\cdot\Big(\frac{u}{\sigma^{2}}\Big)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\Big)du\Bigg)$
$\displaystyle\qquad+\exp\Big(-\frac{c_{2}}{t}-c_{2}\cdot\Big(\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}}\Big)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\Big)$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\Big(-c_{3}\cdot\sigma^{-\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+1}}\Big)+\exp\Big(-c_{3}\cdot\Big(\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}}\Big)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\Big),$
where the passage from the first to the second line is made by integration by parts and the passage to the last line is simply a weighted arithmetic mean-geometric mean inequality. Combining everything, there exists a constant  $c_{4}>0$  such that for  $t$  smaller than some constant,
$\mathbb{P}\Big[T>t\Big]\lesssim\exp\Big(-c_{4}\cdot\sigma^{-\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+1}}\Big)+\exp\left(-c_{4}\left(\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\right).$
Note that this inequality extends to all  $t$  because of the first term which is constant in  $t$  and dominates as long as  $t\gg\sigma^{\gamma/(\gamma+1)}$ . This first term encapsulates the fact that  $T$  may be very large (or even infinite) because  $\langle Z,Z\rangle_{t}$  does not tend to  $\infty$  almost surely, and so this first term is notably a bound for  $\mathbb{P}[T=\infty]$ . Conversely, when  $t\ll\sigma^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+1}}$  (which is much larger than  $\sigma$ ), it is the second term which dominates.
∎
B.3 Large deviation principles for sums of random variables with stretched exponential tails
Finally, in this section, we follow a strategy similar to [4] to prove Lemma 3.7.
Proof of Lemma 3.7.
First start by separating the probability
$\mathbb{P}[X>t]\leq\mathbb{P}\left[\sup_{i}(a_{i}T_{i})>t\right]+\mathbb{P}\left[X>t,\ \sup_{i}(a_{i}T_{i})\leq T\right]$
The first term of the RHS of the above equation can be estimated by a simple union bound, using the fact that  $t\gtrsim S$ :
$\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\sup_{i}(a_{i}T_{i})>t\right]$
$\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{i}\exp\left(-c\left(\frac{t}{a_{i}}\right)^{\gamma}\right)\lesssim\sum_{i}\frac{a_{i}}{S}\exp\left(-\frac{c}{2}\left(\frac{t}{a_{i}}\right)^{\gamma}\right)$
$\displaystyle\leq\exp\left(-\frac{c}{2}\left(\frac{t}{m}\right)^{\gamma}\right).$
We pass to the second term. Here, we introduce a parameter  $\lambda$ , which we set equal to  $\lambda:=\frac{ct^{\gamma-1}}{2m^{\gamma}}$ . Then we may write
$\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[X>t,\ \sup_{i}(a_{i}T_{i})\leq T\right]$
$\displaystyle\leq e^{-\lambda t}\prod_{i}\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\lambda a_{i}T_{i}}\mathbbm{1}(a_{i}T_{i}\leq t)\big]$
$\displaystyle\leq\exp\left(-\lambda t+\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}\big[(e^{\lambda a_{i}T_{i}}-1)\mathbbm{1}(a_{i}T_{i}\leq t)\big]\right).$
We now estimate the expectations inside the exponential. Write  $\mathbb{P}_{T_{i}}$  for the law of  $T_{i}$ , then using integration by parts, one gets (as long as  $t/a_{i}$  is not an atom of  $T_{i}$ , while there are only countably many  $t$  where this can occur),
$\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[(e^{\lambda a_{i}T_{i}}-1)\mathbbm{1}(a_{i}T_{i}\leq t)\big]$
$\displaystyle=\lambda a_{i}\int_{0}^{t/a_{i}}e^{\lambda a_{i}s}\mathbb{P}_{T_{i}}([s,t/a_{i}])ds\lesssim\lambda a_{i}\int_{0}^{t/a_{i}}e^{\lambda a_{i}s-cs^{\gamma}}ds.$
For  $s\leq t/a_{i}$ , one may use that  $0<\gamma<1$  to write that
$\lambda a_{i}s\leq\frac{ct^{\gamma-1}}{2m^{\gamma}}a_{i}\left(\frac{t}{a_{i}}\right)^{1-\gamma}s^{\gamma}\leq\frac{c}{2}s^{\gamma}.$
Hence one may bound the integral  $\int_{0}^{t/a_{i}}e^{\lambda a_{i}s-cs^{\gamma}}ds$  by  $\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-cs^{\gamma}/2}ds$  which is a finite constant depending only on  $c$ . From this, one gets that  $\mathbb{E}[(e^{\lambda a_{i}T_{i}}-1)\mathbbm{1}(a_{i}T_{i}\leq t)]\lesssim\lambda a_{i}$ . Putting everything together and using the value of  $\lambda$ , we obtain
$\mathbb{P}\left[X>t,\ \sup_{i}(a_{i}T_{i})\leq T\right]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{c}{2}\left(\frac{t}{m}\right)^{\gamma}+K\frac{t^{\gamma-1}}{m^{\gamma}}S\right),$
where  $K$  is a constant depending on  $c$ , which can be made explicit depending on  $c$  and the constant of the  $\lesssim$  in the previous equation. Now we set  $C$  to be  $C:=\frac{4K}{c}$  so that if  $t\geq CS$ , one may write  $K\frac{t^{\gamma-1}}{m^{\gamma}}S\leq\frac{c}{4}\left(\frac{t}{m}\right)^{\gamma}$  and therefore for  $t\geq CS$ , one gets
$\mathbb{P}[X>t]\lesssim\exp\left(-\frac{c}{4}\left(\frac{t}{m}\right)^{\gamma}\right).$
This concludes the proof.
∎

Instructions for reporting errors
We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
methods listed below:
Click the "Report Issue" (
) button, located in the page header.
Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.
Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
all.
Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.

our major funders,
member institutions, ,
and all contributors.
